articles.title: Lawsuit tracker: New resistance battling Trump's second term through onslaught of lawsuits taking aim at EOs
articles.summary: Fox New Digital compiled a list of groups, elected officials, individuals and local jurisdictions that have launched lawsuits against the Trump administration over executive actions.
articles.body: Dozens of activist and legal groups, elected officials, local jurisdictions and individuals have launched more than 200 lawsuits against the Trump administration since Jan. 20 in response to his more than 90 executive orders, as well as executive proclamations and memos, Fox News Digital found.  Trump has long been a legal target, which hit a fever pitch during the 2024 election cycle when Trump faced four criminal indictments, including a criminal trial in Manhattan in the spring of 2024 when he was found guilty on 34 counts of falsifying business records.  Trump has maintained his innocence in the four cases, pointing to them as evidence of lawfare at the hands of Democrats working against his political efforts.  Upon Trump's election win in November 2024, state attorneys general, such as New York Attorney General Letitia James, publicly said they would prepare legal battles against the Trump administration for actions they view as illegal or negatively impact residents.  TRUMP HATING NY ATTORNEY GENERAL LETITIA JAMES VOWS WAR WITH PRESIDENT-ELECT IN DIVISIVE NEWS CONFERENCE "We faced this challenge before, and we used the rule of law to fight back," James, who has repeatedly filed suits against Trump, said following his win. "And we are prepared to fight back once again because, as the attorney general of this great state, it is my job to protect and defend the rights of New Yorkers and the rule of law. And I will not shrink from that responsibility." Just weeks back in the Oval Office, Trump's administration has been hit with at least 208 lawsuits working to resist his policies.  Fox News Digital compiled a list of the groups, state attorneys general, cities or states, and individuals who have launched lawsuits against the Trump administration's executive actions. The list includes the various groups and individuals challenging the Trump administration in court, as well as the executive order or proclamation that sparked the suit.  Amid the flurry of lawsuits against Trump and his administration, Democratic elected officials and government employees have spoken out against the orders and the Trump agenda overall.  Democrats and government employees have also staged protests as the Department of Government Efficiency investigates various federal agencies as part of its mission to cut government overspending and weed out corruption and mismanagement of taxpayer funds.  "That's not acceptable," House Minority Leader Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., declared in January. "We are going to fight it legislatively. We are going to fight it in the courts. We're going to fight it in the streets."  'LOSING THEIR MINDS': DEM LAWMAKERS FACE BACKLASH FOR INVOKING 'UNHINGED' VIOLENT RHETORIC AGAINST MUSK "We will see you in the court, in Congress, in the streets," Rep. Ayanna Pressley, D-Mass., said at a rally outside the Treasury Department earlier in February.  "We are gonna be in your face, we are gonna be on your a--es, and we are going to make sure you understand what democracy looks like, and this ain’t it," Rep. Jasmine Crockett, D-Texas, said at the same rally.  TRUMP 100% DISAGREES WITH FEDERAL JUDGE'S 'CRAZY' RULING BLOCKING DOGE FROM TREASURY SYSTEM Trump joined Fox News' Bret Baier for an exclusive interview ahead of the Super Bowl on Feb. 9, where he was asked about a lawsuit filed by attorneys general to restrict DOGE and its chair, Elon Musk, from accessing the Treasury Department's systems and a judge temporarily blocking the DOGE team from the data.  "Nineteen states attorneys general filed a lawsuit, and early Saturday a judge agreed with them to restrict Elon Musk and his government efficiency team, DOGE, from accessing Treasury Department payment and data systems. They said there was a risk of ‘irreparable harm.’ What do you make of that?" Baier asked Trump in the interview clip. "And does that slow you down and what you want to do?"  "No, I disagree with it 100%," Trump said. "I think it's crazy. And we have to solve the efficiency problem. We have to solve the fraud, waste, abuse, all the things that have gone into the government. You take a look at the USAID, the kind of fraud in there."   CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP "We're talking about hundreds of millions of dollars of money that's going to places where it shouldn't be going," Trump said when asked about what DOGE has found while auditing federal agencies in search of government overspending, fraud and corruption. This tracker will be updated with additional lawsuits as they are confirmed.

articles.title: ICE begins new, nationwide effort to arrest illegal aliens at immigration hearings
articles.summary: Sources in the DHS tell Fox News Digital that ICE officers are starting to arrest illegal immigrants when they make court appearances for asylum hearings.
articles.body: Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers have launched a nationwide initiative to begin arresting illegal immigrants at their immigration and asylum hearings, Fox News has learned. The effort targets illegal immigrants who have been in the U.S. fewer than two years. The DHS strategy is to drop their immigration case, arrest the migrant, then place them into expedited deportation proceedings. The initiative requires the DHS to drop the cases because migrants cannot be put forward for expedited removal if they have a pending case. ICE sources who spoke with Fox News Digital on condition of anonymity say Americans should expect to see "a lot more" of these kinds of arrests. HOUSE GOP TARGETS ANOTHER DEM OFFICIAL ACCUSED OF BLOCKING ICE AMID DELANEY HALL FALLOUT The new policy is likely to lead to a spike in deportations of migrants who have not committed crimes aside from crossing the U.S.-Mexico border illegally. The Trump administration has so far focused its efforts on deporting illegal immigrants who have been convicted of other serious crimes. News of the policy comes as the Department of Homeland Security is in multiple court battles regarding its deportation efforts. A federal judge on Wednesday ruled that the DHS had violated a court order in sending a plane full of eight illegal immigrants to South Sudan this week. U.S. District Judge Brian Murphy ruled that the migrants — all of whom are convicted of crimes ranging from homicide to robbery — were not properly given "credible fear interviews." The interviews allow migrants being deported to a third-party country to argue that being sent there would endanger them. Murphy said he is investigating whether the deportees can conduct their interviews in South Sudan rather than returning to the U.S. immediately. CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP Murphy previously found that any plans to deport people to Libya without notice would "clearly" violate his ruling regarding third-party deportations, which also applies to people who have otherwise exhausted their legal appeals.

articles.title: College Republicans of America stands by new political director amid scrutiny of past controversial comments
articles.summary: The College Republicans of America face backlash after appointing Kai Schwemmer as political director after his past controversial statements came to light.
articles.body: The College Republicans of America (CRA) is facing backlash after appointing Kai Schwemmer as its new political director, with critics pointing to his past controversial statements and ties to figures associated with the "groyper" movement. Schwemmer, who was tapped by the CRA for a leadership role earlier this month, has ties to far-right influencer Nick Fuentes and has made numerous statements that some critics described as antisemitic.  He also has a channel on Cozy.Tv, a platform founded by Fuentes and Alex Jones. While the channel appears to be actively gaining followers, the last video listed under the "replays" section was from June 2025. Schwemmer appeared in a 2021 video promoting Fuentes' "White Boy Summer" tour and was a "special guest" at Fuentes' 2022 America First Political Action Conference, according to Jewish Insider. UNIVERSITY OF FLORIDA DISCRIMINATED AGAINST COLLEGE REPUBLICANS CHAPTER, ATTORNEY CLAIMS In a December interview with Reawaken USA, Schwemmer claimed that the CEOs of Raytheon and Boeing were Jewish, grouping them in with "Zionists in America" who would back U.S. involvement in and support of Israel "no matter what," even though neither of the top executives are Jewish.  When asked about his comments, a representative for CRA said Schwemmer's "intention was not to be antisemitic or incorrect, but rather that he’d encountered false information while researching." The College Republicans of America was formed in 2023 amid a disagreement with establishment leadership at the College Republican National Committee. Its goal is to "aid the GOP in cultivating the next generation of Republican activists, staffers, and leaders." Several Jewish organizations, like the ADL and StopAntisemitism, condemned Schwemmer’s appointment, citing his controversial past. "Fuentes holds strong influence over his fans, the 'Groyper Army,' and regularly jokes about the Holocaust. Schwemmer has appeared at Fuentes' conferences, streams on his platform and has spread conspiracy theories about 'Zionists' in America," Anti-Defamation League CEO Jonathan Greenblatt wrote on X.  "At a time when we have witnessed the real dangers of antisemitism in higher education and know there is a clear and growing problem on campuses, elevating individuals who promote this kind of hate-filled rhetoric undermines the credibility of the organization and the values it claims to uphold," StopAntisemitism founder and Executive Director Liora Rez said in a statement to Fox News Digital. Schwemmer, who studies at Brigham Young University in Utah, issued a statement March 13 saying his past remarks did not reflect his current beliefs. "Life is a process of growth and refinement. My comments in high school and as a teenager should not be taken to accurately reflect my views or demeanor now. I condemn all forms of hatred, including antisemitism, obviously," Schwemmer wrote on X in a direct response to Greenblatt.  "I’m not a groyper; I am simply and unapologetically an American nationalist. Additionally, all positions I hold are personal ones, not those of the CRA. I reject the ADL’s allegation that the College Republicans or I currently hate or have ever hated Jews." Schwemmer acknowledged that, in the past, he spoke "in ways that were unnecessarily crass or demeaning," adding that "since returning from my service as a missionary, I have made adjustments to become a better disciple of Christ." He did not elaborate in the post about which opinions had changed or to what specific remarks he was referring.  MARYLAND WOMAN SAYS TPUSA HIGH SCHOOL EVENT RAISED 'SERIOUS CONCERNS,' SAYS CHILD PROTECTIVE SERVICES NOTIFIED CRA's leadership did not back down when faced with mounting criticism. CRA President Martin Bertao said he would not apologize for choosing Schwemmer. "Over the last day I have done a lot of reflecting on my decision to appoint Kai as CRA’s political director. And in that reflection I have came [sic] to the decision that I would like to apologize… to absolutely NOBODY, CRA will never back down to the WOKE mob!" he wrote March 6. Bertao responded to Schwemmer's statement, saying he looked forward to the new political director playing a key role in CRA's efforts to help support Republicans in the midterm elections.  Schwemmer is also listed as a speaker for Turning Point USA's Pick Up the Mic initiative, which was started to honor the memory of TPUSA founder Charlie Kirk. Turning Point USA didn't respond for comment.  JEWISH GROUP DEMANDS FIRING OF BROADCASTER WHO CALLED 'ZIONIST' ISRAELI OLYMPIAN SUPPORTER OF 'GENOCIDE' In response to Fox News Digital's inquiries about Schwemmer and the controversy surrounding his appointment, Macy Gunnell, CRA's vice president of communications, pointed to a letter released by CRA Chairman William Donahue saying that "we are moving forward now not feeding into any divisions among the Right, and instead focusing all of that energy on campaigning and electing Republicans." Schwemmer echoed this sentiment in his statement to Fox News Digital, saying, "I, along with the rest of the college Republicans, are done feeding into the 'eat your own' cancel culture paradigm of division that only seeks to advantage the left. We’re interested in constructing a better future for Americans, and every minute spent focusing on quote-mining and drama is a minute not spent fighting to pass legislation like the Save America Act which will have a real effect on the nation's trajectory." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Schwemmer was critical last month of President Donald Trump over his administration's handling of the Epstein files. "We started out not trusting the government, so we voted for Trump and for something new," he told The New York Times. "And now, we’re watching him turn into the same thing we’ve had for all this time. If a populist, right-wing president is not to be trusted, what does that leave you with?"

articles.title: WATCH: Hearing turmoil as Jasmine Crockett unloads on MLK's niece in wild racially-charged rant
articles.summary: Rep. Jasmine Crockett accused Republicans of using Alveda King as a prop to shield racism allegations during an SPLC hearing on hate group funding.
articles.body: Rep. Jasmine Crockett erupted at Republicans, calling them a "majority… White" party and accusing them of using a member of Martin Luther King Jr.’s family as a prop to shield themselves from allegations of racism while interrogating the Southern Poverty Law Center's funding of hate groups. Crockett, who is leaving office next year after a failed Senate bid, lambasted Republicans for expressing outrage at the SPLC while not addressing the "literal elephant in the room" — a reference to Martin Luther King Jr.’s more conservative niece, Alveda King. Crockett disparaged civil rights activist Alveda King as a right-wing prop while accusing Republicans of trying to trick the public into thinking a "Doctor King" was criticizing the SPLC’s work. King later questioned whether Crockett was calling her a "bastard" of the King name. "The vast majority on that side of the aisle… are White men. White men are lecturing people of color because the vast majority, actually any semblance of diversity comes from this [Democratic] side of the aisle," Crockett said. FIRST ON FOX: SPLC'S TAX-EXEMPT STATUS UNDER THREAT AFTER FIERY CAPITOL HILL HEARING She said people of color don’t feel welcome in the GOP and "that’s why you have to parade someone who has the name ‘Doctor King’ attached to them so people can be confused." Notably, GOP Rep. Wesley Hunt, a fellow Black Texan, was on the committee’s dais and pointedly questioned SPLC leader Bryan Fair earlier in the day. Hunt often rebukes talk of race-based partisanship by quipping that he has been "Black my entire life." Crockett said Republicans were hypocritical in accusing the SPLC of funding hate groups, citing a debunked assertion about President Donald Trump’s comments following the 2017 White supremacist rally in Charlottesville. She noted Trump had said there were "fine people on both sides," but omitted that he later clarified he was referring to a community group opposing the removal of Gen. Robert E. Lee’s statue, a gathering that occurred before the neo-Nazi violence erupted later that day. Crockett then claimed people on social media were wondering who the "Doctor King" was who was speaking out against the SPLC as the hearing progressed, and that Republicans were trying to make the public think the historic Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. would be on their side. NEARLY ALL SUSPECTS ARRESTED IN ST. PAUL CHURCH STORMING AS MLK’S NIECE SAYS TACTICS ‘NOT THE WAY’ Crockett said Republicans would be better served calling the Obama-supporting Martin Luther King III or his sister Bernice King to the hearing — suggesting they understand the civil rights icon’s teachings and positions better than Alveda. Before her time expired, she accused King and Republicans of "caping" for murdered activist Charlie Kirk — quoting a controversial statement by the Turning Point USA founder about the Civil Rights Act. She also claimed Republicans hauled Fair and King before the committee because they wanted to distract from their failure to hold a hearing examining associates of deceased financier and convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. articles.title: Chris Mason: What his first week in power tells us about Andy Burnham
articles.summary: The fledgling Burnham administration has been seeking to find its feet and make a decent first impression at the same time, the BBC's political editor Chris Mason explains.
articles.body:
"We are on borrowed time if we don't get a move on," Angela Rayner, the former deputy prime minister who is back in the cabinet this week as housing secretary, told the BBC's Today programme on Friday.

It has been quite the week at Westminster. Sir Keir Starmer's departure as prime minister on Monday seems rather a while ago.

The fledgling Burnham administration has been seeking to find its feet and make a decent first impression at the same time, as many try to do in the first days in a job.

There has been an early pattern in these early days: an early morning nugget of news dropping from No10.

On Thursday, it was business rates in England ; on Wednesday, it was bus fares in England and on Tuesday, it was a VAT cut on electricity bills .

Today, the prime minister is assembling what Rayner calls "a pride of mayors" among others for a meeting of what is known as the National Economic Council at the new No 10 North in Manchester.

Andy Burnham claims his new base in Manchester represents the beginning of " the biggest rebalancing of power our country has seen , external " and he will be "bringing forward the biggest changes in the last 40 years".

His early announcements have been considerably more piecemeal than that â he says his "10 year plan for Britain" will come later in the year.

It is worth remembering there was talk from both Boris Johnson and his allies and from Sir Keir Starmer about their plans for the decade ahead â both fizzled out rather more quickly than that.

So how should we assess how much politics has changed, or not?

The early evidence - and let's be frank, it is only that given we are just a few days in - points to Andy Burnham being both more sharp and more nimble than his predecessor in setting out what he is attempting to do and trying to point to early examples of what that might look like, with the announcements of the last few days.

With the tinkering of how the government is run, like the creation of the Office of Prime Minister, and the establishment of No 10 North, he's made it clear that the arteries of power flow very much to and from him.

He hopes he can overcome the critique of Sir Keir Starmer and others, that one of the frustrations of being prime minister can be pulling levers and nothing actually happens.

Burnham's opponents are having to recalibrate and work through how they take on a new prime minister.

The Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch's al fresco speech and news conference on a rooftop in central London on Thursday was a tacit acknowledgement that the political terms of trade have changed.

She teased the new prime minister over his informal style â he "seems like a nice guyâ¦I'm glad he's got a sense of humour," she told us, before getting to the essence of her critique, that his offer was superficial, and thin.

"Is that it?" she asked, adding: "He is behaving like he's still the mayor of Manchester. He is now the prime minister of the United Kingdom."

Burnham wants to project a sense that he gets it - the cost of living pressures so many feel so acutely - and he is getting a move on.

But in just these first few days there has been a reminder that life comes at you fast as prime minister.

Firstly, on the domestic front â his intervention on the early release of prisoners in England and Wales, demanding what he calls a "pause", is a case study in the dilemmas of governing: crowded prisons and, so, difficult choices between least worst options â which criminals to free first.

Secondly, on the international front â after Burnham renewed America's permission to use British airbases for what are called "defensive" strikes on Iran, Tehran is claiming those bases are now legitimate targets. And, with the conflict in the Middle East escalating, the oil price is spiking again .

Then there are the huge questions that tumble from Burnham's big promises.

He has pledged, for instance, "the biggest council house building programme since the post war period." How would this be paid for? And what does the promise actually mean?

It is worth a listen to Matt Chorley's interview with Angela Rayner on BBC Radio 5 Live on precisely this point - the housing secretary isn't able to define when the "post war period" ended and therefore there is no numerical target attached to what appears to be a rather bold promise.

And this on the same day that Rayner acknowledging keeping Labour's promise to build 1.5 million new homes in England by 2029 looks rather shaky: she told the BBC it was "a difficult target".

What about defence spending? The new chancellor, John Healey, packed it in as defence secretary because he thought the department he now runs, the Treasury, didn't get it when it came to keeping us safe.

Let's see how he gets on now the boot is on the other foot.

Burnham is cutting business rates for some in England, but what of Labour's promise in its manifesto two years ago to "replace the business rates system, so we can raise the same revenue but in a fairer way." Will that happen?

And beyond the symbolism of having a prime ministerial office outside London, what, in practical terms, can No10 North actually achieve? How much clout and authority is it given? Just how often will senior ministers be there? And how much will it cost?

Civil servants are being asked if they would like to relocate to the north west of England. The indications from Team Burnham is they take it hugely seriously, but does the civil service truly respond to that, and given the turbulence in politics in recent years, is it an idea that lives beyond this prime minister?

Given the intended long term home of No 10 North is currently a building site and is not due to be finished until 2032 , this is a live question.

Sackings, cabinet surprises and policies: Burnham's first 24 hours as PM Published 21 July

Sackings, cabinet surprises and policies: Burnham's first 24 hours as PM

Senior ministers and aides set to work from No 10 North Published 23 July

Senior ministers and aides set to work from No 10 North

Burnham has big ideas - but what will they cost? Published 20 July

Burnham has big ideas - but what will they cost?

And how many noises off do we hear from grumpy Starmerites as the early novelty of governing dilutes? Given the speed with which one, Darren Jones, went public with a grumble it will be something Team Burnham will be wary of.

Then, there is the new prime minister's boldest claim of all â that he will be "bringing forward the biggest changes in the last 40 years". Really? He describes a desire for a "new political model and a new economic model".

It is an understatement to say this triggers a cascade of questions. Including, for some of his critics, including Reform UK, a key one â where is your mandate for doing this?

The fascinating question of the coming months is the extent to which Andy Burnham can credibly or not, as voters see it, set a pathway towards the change he wants and then, in time, call a general election asking for an endorsement of his ideas and direction.

It is three years until there has to be an election, but the timing up until then is in his gift.

His opponents are publicly saying bring it on when there is talk of an election sooner rather than later. Privately, plenty of Conservative and Reform folk acknowledge they are not ready yet.

Could Andy Burnham be tempted? When asked, he has said "we're in a parliamentary democracy and, as we've seen through time, if somebody can command a majority of the MPs in the House of Commons, they obviously then have the legitimacy to lead things forward." That is a statement of constitutional truth, rather than a definitive answer either way to the question itself.

Many prime ministers arriving in office between general elections crave their own mandate. Gordon Brown reflects in his memoirs the agonising private conversations he had about a snap election and in deciding against it found himself going "from near hero to near zero in a day."

Boris Johnson went for it in 2019 and got a near-landslide out of it.

Theresa May, on the other hand, went for it in 2017 and ended up losing the majority she had inherited. The recent history books, then, offer a less than clear guide and Burnham has inherited a colossal majority.

His decision and its timing will likely be driven by how quickly and how much he can do with it.

In other words, whether he is popular enough.

articles.title: Greens review social media operation as Polanski row rumbles on
articles.summary: The Green Party is grappling with how to manage its social media following a controversial post by its leader.
articles.body:
The Green Party of England and Wales is reviewing its social media operation which has been central to its surge in popularity over the past year, sources have told the BBC.

They insist it is not connected to the backlash to Zack Polanski this week after he re-posted a photo of a man wearing a t-shirt with an image of a guillotine and the slogan "we're only making plans for Nigel" - seen as being a reference to Nigel Farage.

But that incident has raised questions about whether it is sustainable for the Green Party leader to manage his own social media channels, with one party figure calling it an "avoidable mistake" and that Polanski "should have said sorry" for it.

In an interview with BBC Newsnight, Polanski repeatedly refused to apologise for "an inadvertent mistake" but acknowledged he needed to "be better on social media".

"I just didn't look carefully enough and I accepted it, as soon as I was aware of what happened I unaccepted it and took it down," he said.

Like other high profile figures on social media, Polanski receives a lot of material from other users seeking re-posts. But unlike most political leaders in the UK, he still manages his own accounts, rather than handing control to party staffers.

This may allow him to appear spontaneous and authentic - both valuable commodities on social media - but it comes with risks.

The current row began after Polanski shared a single post on Instagram that contained a carousel of 20 pictures.

The re-post was shared to Polanski's 713,000 followers, because he accepted a request to tag him as a collaborator, which on the platform makes him a "co-author," placing it on his page and into his followers' feeds.

Polanski said he had not noticed the offending image among the others on the post.

According to him, he had accepted collaborator tags for eight other posts from the same event in Bristol alone.

Reform UK leader Farage claimed the t-shirt amounted to incitement to murder and his party reported it to the police.

Neither the Metropolitan Police nor Avon and Somerset Police say the incident meets the threshold for further action .

But the political row has continued with Reform UK MP Robert Jenrick calling Polanski a "nasty piece of work", at a news conference earlier on Thursday.

Inside the Green Party, there has been some criticism of Polanski's behaviour online.

He has attracted positive and negative attention for the rate at which he posts, comments, likes and replies across multiple platforms including X, Bluesky, Facebook and Instagram.

And this is not the first time a quick reaction has attracted controversy; last month he had to apologise to police after posting about their response to the Golders Green attack.

One senior party source said it was clear that due diligence had not been done on Polanski's social media output, and that moving forwards he needs "tight controls" to stay credible, while keeping a similar tone of engagement with his followers.

They pointed out that the speed and number of Polanski's interactions came with a "small upside" but a "colossal downside", and with the latest incident he had "shot himself in the foot at precisely the wrong time".

It comes as recent polling suggests the Green Party has lost ground to Labour, following Andy Burnham's election as Labour leader, and down from a peak earlier this year.

They added their concerns about a wider problem with the party's vetting on social media and of candidates, including around antisemitic posts in recent months.

Several candidates in recent elections have stood down over their social media activity, with two candidates arrested during May's local elections, and another suspended after being elected.

But Green Party peer and former deputy mayor of London Baroness Jones said the criticism of Polanski's Instagram re-post seemed to be "mainly from our opponents, not internal discussions".

She said that her party leader had "made a mistake", adding "we've all done it and got flak."

But she added: "His online presence is what makes him relatable".

Along with relatability, comes popularity: Polanski is the second-most followed UK leader on Instagram after Nigel Farage. The Greens surpassed other parties to become the most popular on the platform this year.

It is also seen as where a good portion of their voters spend time, as they are the most popular party among the under-30s, according to pollsters YouGov.

One party source said there had been discussions among councillors and activists about whether Polanski was "too online".

"Is he just too online? Is he doing it all himself? Where's the professionalisation here, given the level the party's now grown to, and what people expect of us?" they said.

"There's got to be more checks and balances" the source added.

A separate party source confirmed there was a review going on internally into the party's social media operation, but would not be drawn on whether that meant changing who had oversight of Polanski's posts.

"We are looking at our processes and systems in this area," they said.

"Obviously Zack is really active on social media. It is how we have grown our reach and our membership."

Until around a year ago the party's entire social media team consisted of one full-time employee.

That has now gone up to three or four and may increase further following the review.

"We have expanded hugely as a party and we are looking at how we work," the source said.

"As part of that we are looking at what we might do to support and beef up our social media team."

They said the coverage of the Instagram re-post row had been "deeply irritating" but added that the review was not directly linked to that incident.

But it remains to be seen how much longer Polanski can retain control of his accounts before handing over the passwords to party staffers.

articles.title: Colorado's socialist surge shakes up the Democratic establishment
articles.summary: A veteran Colorado political insider warned the democratic socialists' rise in Denver mirrors the MAGA movement and could become a cancer for Democrats.
articles.body: Democratic socialist candidate Melat Kiros shocked Colorado’s Democratic establishment when she defeated 15-term incumbent Rep. Diana DeGette in the state's June primary. The double-digit win exposed a growing rift over the party's values that has left some Democrats stunned and questioning the future of the party. "If you had told me this woman would have won by 13 points, I would have bet my house against that," Doug Friednash, a veteran political strategist in Colorado, told Fox News Digital. "I never would have thought we would have seen a victory of that magnitude here in Denver." Friednash has tracked Colorado's political shift from red to deep blue over the past three decades, previously serving in the state legislature representing House District 10 in Denver. He later served as Denver city attorney and chief of staff to former Colorado Gov. John Hickenlooper, and he currently works as a partner at Brownstein, a prominent legal and lobbying firm in the region. Kiros' victory was one of dozens of wins for far-left candidates in Democratic primary elections this cycle as socialists continue to ascend across the country. The far left's rise in the party has alarmed seasoned Democrats like Friednash. JEWISH COMMUNITY IN DENVER ON HIGH ALERT OVER RISE OF DEMOCRATIC SOCIALIST MELAT KIROS "It was one thing watching this happen in New York. ... But when it happens in a state like Colorado, which is really the gateway to the West, it tells me that this issue is going to spread and may be a cancer to the Democratic Party if they don't figure out what our values are," Friednash said. He noted that Kiros' victory did not happen in a vacuum, pointing out that DSA-backed candidates have successfully captured seats in the state legislature and city councils over the past few years. While Friednash originally predicted Rep. Diana DeGette would win, he acknowledged Kiros' campaign had a strong ground game and was able to tap into anti-establishment sentiments among progressives in the region. Kiros' team reportedly knocked on more than 100,000 voters' doors and ran a phone bank reaching 500,000 people leading up to election night. SOCIALISM’S RISE INSIDE THE DEMOCRATIC PARTY NOW THREATENS THE AMERICAN DREAM She also campaigned on fighting for universal healthcare, affordable housing, utilities and more. Friednash said Kiros' message resonated with younger voters who are frustrated by the high cost of living and feel let down by the Democratic establishment. "I think the number one issue is affordability, by far," he said. "A lot of younger people that have moved to Denver have come here wanting to buy a house. They can't buy a home, it seems unaffordable and unattainable. And I think she's tapped into a lot of voter anger and hostility over things not being better." He believes Denver has become a microcosm of the national debate taking place within the Democratic Party over its future direction. Comparing the Democratic Socialists of America wave to the rise of the MAGA movement within the Republican Party, Friednash warned that if party leadership refuses to call out the group's extreme policies, it will ultimately hurt Democrats in swing districts across the nation. RAHM EMANUEL WARNS DSA AGENDA DOESN'T PLAY WELL OUTSIDE 'UPPER WEST SIDE OF MANHATTAN' "As I look out at what's happening within the Democratic Party, you know, it's kind of like a ship without a captain," Friednash said. "A lot of the more mainstream Democrats, rather than trying to say, 'Here are the issues we should be fighting about,' are embracing the socialists  because I think they're afraid of them ... much like I think we've seen with the MAGA movement. "While some Democrats may be falling in love with socialism, you know who isn't? The rest of America," he continued. "That dog's not gonna hunt in these more competitive primaries." Prominent centrist Democratic groups such as Third Way share that anxiety. The organization recently told The New York Times it plans to launch a $15 million campaign to combat the DSA movement, which it believes poses a "mortal danger" to Democrats and will hurt the party in potential presidential swing states. Concerns over the party's ideological turn aren't limited to establishment Democrats. Jon Caldara, president of the Denver-based free market think tank Independence Institute, also questions the future of his home state as democratic socialists continue to rise in prominence. "Without a doubt, the Democratic Party in Colorado has changed," Caldara told Fox News Digital, arguing the state has abandoned its historically pro-business stance. Caldara, a libertarian and longtime radio host and columnist, is outspoken about the challenges facing Denver and the broader state, such as affordability, homelessness and an exodus of businesses. He believes these issues will worsen, warning that establishment Democrats have lost control of their own party. "When the state started turning left, this machine was so powerful, it really couldn't stop itself," Caldara said. "And now it's really beginning to eat their own. It's kind of a French Revolution thing that you see that the Democratic Party here in Colorado is now well out over their skis. And there is a growing fight between Democrats and socialists. "The real telltale is that Democrats are afraid to speak the truth because they don't want to get canceled," he added. "It is vicious to go against the socialists." SHOCKING PERCENTAGE OF DEMOCRATS IDENTIFY AS 'DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS' ACCORDING TO NEW POLL: 'TOXIC POLICIES' Caldara believes younger voters are increasingly being drawn to democratic socialist candidates in Denver and across the country because they lack historical context for how these types of policies have fared across the world. "Sadly, the young suffer from a terrible disease: It's called youth. And because they're young, they haven't seen failed socialism around the globe," Caldara said. "They haven't seen what happened in the Soviet Union. They haven't learned the lesson of Sweden, which looked like such a wonderful socialist paradise until it didn't work, and now they're turning into a capitalist system. They haven't seen this. "So, the idea that we can just redistribute rich guys' money sounds great," he continued. "We'll just do rent control. We'll do government funding. We all know how that's going to end up. It's going to end up poorly. And young people are going to be hurt. "I'm sad that they want to run this experiment again," he added. "And it's even sadder that it's happening in this beautiful free state, this western state, this pro-free-enterprise state of Colorado." Longtime Colorado residents like Gene Maine understand full well why socialist policies are appealing. But having fled the Soviet Union as a teenager in 1981, Maine sees unsettling parallels between the society he grew up in and the direction Denver is headed. As a child, Maine said he was often told that America, Western Europe and capitalism were evil. But as he got older, he realized the utopian society he was supposedly living in wasn't all that it was cracked up to be. REPUBLICANS SOUND ALARM OVER FAR-LEFT GROUP'S PUSH TO TRANSFORM AMERICA INTO 'CUBAN DICTATORSHIP' "As I grew older, I started recognizing that, ‘Oh my God, I'm being lied to. We're all being lied to," Maine recalled. "This is not the freest society in the world. It's a jail." After defecting from the USSR with his mother as a teenager, Maine lived in Los Angeles before settling in Erie, Colorado, in the 1990s, where he’s lived since, raising his family and working as an engineer. Over the past three decades, Maine has watched Denver change from a small "cow town" into a large municipality and witnessed a corresponding political shift as the population boomed. BERNIE SANDERS, DSA REVEAL DEMANDS FOR DEM PARTY AFTER SOCIALISTS SWEEP NEW YORK ELECTIONS "All of a sudden, it wasn't, 'Can we have the smallest government possible and leave us alone?' It became, 'Well, we need to give you free stuff.' And that's when I started to worry a little bit," Maine said. Maine isn't surprised that veteran Democrats are facing primary threats from the far left, noting that Kiros’ campaign benefited from a well-organized ground game and sweeping promises on healthcare and affordability that drew in younger voters. "She is winning the primary because we have an organized group convincing people that they can have free stuff. You can have free medical care. You can have free supermarkets. You can have free transportation. And it's very appealing," Maine explained. "I like free stuff, but what they forget to tell you is that nothing is really free. As they say, there's no free lunch." SOCIALIST HOUSE CANDIDATE SAYS HE AGREES WITH REPUBLICANS ON 'ONE ISSUE' He believes historical lessons are being lost as generations grow further removed from the realities of the Soviet Union. "So, there is a gap that's being exploited," he continued. "And it's been exploited from internal and from external, because there's a lot of evil forces in the world that do not want America to succeed." While critics view the rise of the DSA as a dangerous departure from American values, Kiros and other DSA candidates argue their policies are a pragmatic response to liberal voters fed up with how the Democratic Party has responded to their struggles. Kiros recently brushed aside concerns regarding communists inside the DSA faction of the Democratic Party, telling PBS "Firing Line" host Margaret Hoover there is room in the party for various viewpoints. "Yeah. Well, some members of the Democratic Party are proudly proclaiming themselves as capitalists, and it’s a big tent, right?" Kiros said. "But, again, at the end of the day, it’s up to the voters, right? "Until a self-proclaimed communist actually wins an election, then it’s just noise from the Republican Party. There’s no one who’s actually winning with that." CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE Kiros denied being a communist herself, arguing that younger voters are embracing the DSA message because, at its core, it represents "economic populism." Her campaign centered on Medicare for all, universal childcare, investments in public housing, higher federal taxes on the wealthy, publicly owned utilities and more. Like many other socialist campaigns across the country, she is also firmly anti-Israel.  Kiros' campaign was backed by several progressive groups, including the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), Justice Democrats and the Working Families Party. Republican candidate Christy Peterson, a local accountant, is also running in the Nov. 3 general election, which Kiros is widely expected to win given the district's strongly blue lean. In 2024, Kamala Harris won 77% of the vote in the district en route to winning Colorado. articles.title: Gov. Josh Shapiro issues a new executive order on data centers in Pennsylvania
articles.summary: Shapiro, a potential Democratic 2028 contender, earlier welcomed data center developments. His new executive order takes a starkly different tone toward the industry.
articles.body: Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro announced significant restrictions on data center projects Tuesday, signing an executive order to stop “predatory” backers and “bad proposals from infecting our commonwealth.” The order, along with the warnings in his remarks for potential data center developers, marked a notable shift for Shapiro, a potential 2028 Democratic presidential contender, who had sought to encourage the industry’s build-out in his state. “I’ve heard loud and clear from the good people of Pennsylvania as I’ve traveled our commonwealth, and I’m here to say today that we will not be bullied by these developers,” Shapiro said. “We will not be bulldozed by the lawyers working for these big tech companies. That will not happen in the commonwealth. We have a long history in Pennsylvania of industry running roughshod over our communities to make a buck — that stops with me.” The new order mandates that data center projects must first be approved by local officials. Developers must also sign a legally binding order in which they commit to guidelines Shapiro laid out in February — which were first reported by NBC News — among them that they pay for their own power, hire locally, be transparent with local governments and adhere to high water-conservation standards. Shapiro also said that he is removing all data center projects from his state’s fast-track permitting program and that going forward, they would be ineligible for those measures. He also said nondisclosure agreements for data center projects will not be allowed in the state under his new order. Shapiro said in his remarks that since it announced two major data center projects in the state last year — Amazon-backed developments he touted — the state has “seen an unacceptable number of speculative proposals for data centers swamp our commonwealth — many of them led by developers who have no regard for local communities.” Shapiro, who also faces re-election this fall, has evolved his views on data centers within the last year as the projects have faced increasing opposition in the state and nationally. Last week, The Philadelphia Inquirer wrote about how Shapiro’s early embrace of the projects was testing his high approval ratings with voters who are skeptical of the developments. Even in announcing guidelines this year to manage the data center boom, Shapiro framed the need for Pennsylvania “to play a leading role” in the battle for AI supremacy against China. He said that “no sector of our country’s economy is growing faster than data centers and artificial intelligence,” though the U.S. needed to be “selective” about the projects it pursued. He took a much different tone Tuesday, criticizing “speculators” in the industry for “scaring our communities” and “being aggressive with township officials, bullying our neighbors, our fellow Pennsylvanians, and refusing to listen to the people.” “They’re threatening to fundamentally change the character of our communities,” he said, adding that the lack of legislative progress on passing new regulations for data center development — Pennsylvania’s Legislature is under split control — left him no choice but to move on the executive order. He called out specific data center proposals he has opposed, one of them in Montgomery County, where he lives, saying a developer was trying to “bully his way into forcing data center projects through local opposition from the community and local officials.” “I’m a hell no on that project,” he said, adding, “I’m a hell no on many other projects.” Repeatedly, he credited his evolution on data centers to conversations he has had with concerned Pennsylvania residents, saying the “feedback I’ve gotten ... has shaped my perspective on this.” Democrats and Republicans both are recalibrating on data center development as opposition has ramped up across the midterm landscape. Opponents have expressed concerns about the potential for rising power bills, environmental worries or fears over the growth of AI technology, among other concerns. In New York, Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul last month signed a moratorium on data center development, while in Texas, Republican Gov. Greg Abbott paused data center projects this month pending an audit. In multiple contested general election fights across the map, candidates are battling over whether they support full-scale moratoriums on the developments, favor greater local control or want to extend incentives for further development. The rapid growth of data centers, which are needed to power the AI boom, has been a core component of President Donald Trump’s economic agenda. His administration has promoted the “Ratepayer Protection Pledge,” in which developers who have signed on fund the cost of increased power generation and infrastructure for the developments. Trump has in recent weeks argued for voters to give the developments a warmer embrace, touting benefits that come with them. The industry has pointed to potential job growth and increased tax revenue for localities that accept the developments, as well as potential property tax cuts, among other incentives. Leaders have also argued that environmental concerns have been overblown or are based on faulty data. “Part of the challenge here is how quickly the industry has moved,” Dan Diorio, executive vice president of state policy and government affairs for the Data Center Coalition, said in a recent interview. “And so the opposition, I think, has moved just as quickly,” he added. “Now it’s coming upon us and certainly others to bring the facts and the data to bear but also be out there and demonstrate how this industry invests in the communities for the long term.” Following his announcement Tuesday, Shapiro was asked whether he regretted his state’s earlier approach to data center development. “Again, there are only about five projects that have even received permits to go forward,” he said. “The problem is there’s 100 projects or so that are wreaking havoc on our communities that are never going to be built. What we’re doing today is taking concrete action to listen to the voices of the people, to put local leaders back in charge of their communities and to make very, very clear what the rules of the road are to be able to do business here in Pennsylvania.”

articles.title: Trump nominates Heidi Overton to lead the FDA
articles.summary: Overton, a physician, is a White House aide who often briefs the president on health issues.
articles.body: President Donald Trump will nominate Dr. Heidi Overton to be his new Food and Drug Administration commissioner, he said Wednesday on social media. “Dr. Heidi has been a ROCKSTAR in my Administration,” Trump wrote. Overton, a physician, is a White House domestic policy official who regularly briefs the president on various health issues. She was at his side earlier this month when he announced an executive order aimed at reducing the number of universally recommended childhood vaccinations. At the time, she urged “blue states” to adopt the administration’s “gold standard” recommendations, which many doctors said were not supported by current science. Trump referred to the event in his post announcing the pick. “Heidi is “ALWAYS RIGHT,” Secretary Kennedy recently said in the Oval Office!” he posted. “We need her leadership at the FDA now to ensure that the U.S. remains the WORLD LEADER for Scientific Discovery and CURES.” According to a senior administration official with knowledge of the process, Overton was Trump’s third choice for the position, and the administration was still interviewing candidates for the role Tuesday. Former Rep. Brad Wenstrup, R-Ohio, declined the job, the official said, as did acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas, citing his young children and other personal reservations. If Overton is confirmed by the Senate, she would lead the agency at a delicate time, with the recent multistate cyclospora outbreak raising concerns about the safety of the nation’s food supply. Sen. Bill Cassidy, R-La., the chair of the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee, which will oversee Overton’s nomination, said he has “strong concerns.” “Her lack of managerial experience does not prepare her well for leading a large organization that is already dealing with staffing and morale issues. Additionally, Dr. Overton’s active role in last week’s nonsensical vaccine executive order calls into question her commitment to standing up for sound science and protecting children’s health. That alone is almost disqualifying,” Cassidy wrote on X. Sen. Patty Murray, D-Wash., who is also on the Senate HELP Committee, called Overton a “far-right, anti-abortion extremist who has no business leading the FDA.” “The American people deserve someone who will put science and facts FIRST, not another Trump sycophant who will make it their mission to attack medication abortion. I will vote NO,” Murray said on X. Republicans have a one-member majority in the committee, which must advance the nomination to the full Senate for a vote. Bloomberg was the first to report that Overton would be Trump’s FDA pick. The timing of the official announcement is unclear but is likely to be sometime this week. Overton would replace Dr. Marty Makary, who resigned from the position in May after clashes with the White House over issues like vaping policy and access to abortion pills. She previously served as vice chair and chief policy officer of the America First Policy Institute, a conservative think tank. While there, Overton celebrated the Supreme Court’s 2022 decision that overturned Roe v. Wade and with it a national right to abortion. The ruling “will allow Americans to reevaluate the value of the potential of every baby in the womb and choose life through a democratic process,” she said in a statement at the time. In a 2024 op-ed in Newsweek, Overton criticized Kamala Harris — then vice president and the Democratic nominee for president — because she “refused to condemn late-term abortion,” adding that Democrats “won’t even define what a woman is.” The FDA is conducting a safety review of the abortion pill mifepristone but has not yet issued a report. Republicans have been pushing to reverse a Biden-era rule that allows mifepristone to be mailed and dispensed via telehealth, not just in person. The agency is also in the mix as the Trump administration seeks to make changes to the nation’s vaccine policies. As a White House adviser, Overton participated in Trump’s signing last week of an executive order aimed at reducing the number of standard childhood vaccinations from 18 to 11. In remarks at the Oval Office event, Overton criticized “blue states” that work with outside entities like the American Academy of Pediatrics and recommend what she considered outdated shot recommendations. “So you are saying, especially to states that are willing, take a look at this scientific assessment; these are the gold standard childhood vaccine recommendations, and you should put this into your state law so that when parents go to enroll their kids in school, they do not have to meet some of the requirements for the vaccines that are no longer recommended for all children,” she said. According to Overton’s profile on the America First Policy Institute website, she is board-certified in public health and general preventive medicine, was a general surgery resident at the Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine and completed medical school at the University of New Mexico School of Medicine.

articles.title: Burnham announces plans to clean up worst three illegal waste dumps
articles.summary: The government says the sites in Kent, Surrey and West Yorkshire contain 22,000 tonnes of waste.
articles.body:
Three of the country's worst illegal dumps are due to be cleaned up using taxpayers' money, the government has announced.

Sites in Kent, Surrey and West Yorkshire will be assessed for clearance, with Prime Minister Andy Burnham saying the "toxic dumps have blighted communities for too long".

Fines for waste offences will also rise from Â£300 to Â£5,000 to deter, catch, and punish those who dump illegally, and the Environment Agency will have more powers to seize assets bought with the proceeds of crime by those involved.

But opposition parties said illegal dumps were a small part of a much bigger issue with smaller scale fly-tipping and landfill all posing big problems for communities.

Burnham is looking to build on work started by his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer to tackle waste crime, with an action plan published in March detailing a series of measures - including using drones to map illegal waste sites.

Sir Keir's administration had announced that sites in Wigan, Sheffield and Lancashire would have government clean-ups - alongside Kidlington in Oxfordshire where removal of 20,000 tonnes of waste started in April .

The government said the new sites identified for clearance contain around 22,000 tonnes of illegally dumped waste.

They are: Power Station Road, on the Isle of Sheppey, Kent; Aymer Close, in Runnymede, Surrey; and Midland Road in Bradford, West Yorkshire.

West Yorkshire and Greater Manchester will be the first areas with new region-led approaches to waste crime.

The government said this will give mayors and council leaders the lead in co-ordinating councils, police, regulators, and other enforcement agencies.

Speaking on a visit to the waste dump in West Yorkshire, Burnham said: "We've begun a much more networked approach to this, where we're bringing the National Crime Agency in to work with the Environment Agency, increasing the penalties and bearing down now on the organised crime that lies behind some of what you see behind me."

The prime minister said the aim was to build intelligence about criminals linked to waste dumps at an earlier stage, to avoid the public being charged for clean-ups.

"We should be getting in much earlier, apprehending them, using all of the intelligence that comes through that investigation to make sure the polluter pays," he added.

A new "waste crime crackdown group", chaired by Environment Secretary Angela Eagle, will bring regulators and law enforcement together in a bid to dismantle criminal operations.

Eagle said: "We are cleaning up sites, but we are also stopping the cycle, driving faster prevention and disruption, better intelligence, and stronger coordination across the system."

Police-style powers to tackle fly-tippers being considered

Hundreds of illegal waste tips operating in England - including 11 'super sites' Published 23 January

Hundreds of illegal waste tips operating in England - including 11 'super sites'

City sees more than 16 fly-tipping incidents a day Published 14 March

City sees more than 16 fly-tipping incidents a day

Kevin McKenna, Labour MP for Sittingbourne and Sheppey, one of the clean-up sites, welcomed the announcement, saying: "I want to see that momentum continue, with sites cleared, our environment protected and local people able to take pride in their community again."

A Green Party spokesperson agreed a crackdown was needed, but highlighted that smaller-scale dumping was a bigger issue and called for extra ring-fenced funding.

"We also need to boost the circular economy, so households and businesses are better able to reuse, repair, repurpose and recycle goods and make manufacturers and producers responsible for the safe disposal for the goods and packaging they produce," they added.

Liberal Democrat environment spokesperson Tim Farron welcomed tougher fines but said waste crime was only one part of a bigger problem, and called for an independent review of the waste system.

"Andy Burnham needs to wake up and smell the landfill," he said.

"New mayoral powers won't cut it if the National Crime Agency isn't empowered to clear these illegal sites, and stop legal sites spiralling out of control.

"We need an independent review of the whole system to crack down on these organised gangs once and for all."

The Conservatives and Reform UK have been contacted for comment.

articles.title: Trump reveals exact number of North Korea's nuclear weapons
articles.summary: Trump cited 57 nuclear weapons in North Korea's arsenal, marking the first time a U.S. official has publicly put an exact number on Pyongyang's stockpile.
articles.body: President Donald Trump said Wednesday that North Korea possesses 57 nuclear weapons as he previewed a possible meeting with leader Kim Jong Un later this year. Trump made the remark while defending his relationship with Kim, arguing that his rapport with the North Korean leader is "a good thing," not a bad one. Trump’s unusually precise figure appears to be the first time a U.S. official has publicly put an exact number on North Korea’s nuclear arsenal. Public assessments have generally estimated that Pyongyang has roughly 50 to 60 assembled warheads, while warning that the country’s secretive program makes a definitive count impossible. It was not immediately clear whether Trump’s specific figure was based on a classified U.S. intelligence assessment. TRUMP ORDERS MAJOR CUT TO US-SOUTH KOREA DRILLS AS NORTH KOREA RAMPS UP MISSILE TESTS Trump said Kim is "a very powerful player" and blamed prior administrations for allowing North Korea to develop a nuclear arsenal. "The fact that I get along with him, that’s a good thing," Trump said. "You can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon. And I know Kim Jong Un very well, and he’s going to be fine as long as we have a smart president." Trump said he expected to meet with Kim later this year, though he did not provide a date or location. NORTH KOREA EXPERT WARNS US CAN 'NEVER TAKE THEIR EYE OFF' KIM JONG UN FOLLOWING MISSILE TEST DURING IRAN WAR North Korea’s nuclear stockpile is closely guarded, and public estimates vary. The Federation of American Scientists estimated in 2024 that Pyongyang may have assembled roughly 50 nuclear warheads, while possessing enough fissile material for up to 90. Trump’s comment came after he ordered War Secretary Pete Hegseth this week to substantially scale back the annual U.S.-South Korea Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises, arguing that the drills were costly and sent an "inappropriate and hostile" signal to North Korea. The U.S. and South Korean militaries said Wednesday they would shorten the exercises and end them Friday. The decision is one of several overtures Trump has made toward Kim as he seeks to revive diplomacy with Pyongyang. Trump has said he expects to meet with Kim later this year, potentially during a planned November trip to Asia, though no summit has been announced. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Kim’s sister, Kim Yo Jong, dismissed the reduction in drills as insufficient, saying Washington’s policy toward North Korea remains hostile. Trump and Kim met three times during Trump’s first term, but their negotiations broke down in 2019 without an agreement to curb North Korea’s nuclear program. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP North Korea’s arsenal remains far smaller than those of the world’s two largest nuclear powers. Russia has about 4,400 nuclear warheads in its military stockpile, while the United States has 3,700, according to January estimates by the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute. China has 620, followed by France with 290, the United Kingdom with 225, India with 190, Pakistan with 170 and Israel with 90. SIPRI estimated North Korea has about 60 assembled warheads — broadly in line with Trump’s figure — while cautioning that the secrecy surrounding Pyongyang’s program makes precise counts uncertain.

articles.title: Luxury travel, shopping, six-figure income: Battleground Dems ripped for 'phony' working-class narrative
articles.summary: Dems running in battleground districts criticized over middle-class bios they are presenting to voters as financial records and other materials paint a picture of wealth others don't often have.
articles.body: Several battleground Democrats running in competitive House races have leaned on working-class, blue-collar biographies to connect with voters’ economic anxieties, but financial records and other materials reviewed by Fox News Digital complicate the images they have presented on the campaign trail. In New Jersey, for example, Democratic Party candidate Rebecca Bennett has pitched herself as a parent with firsthand understanding of the "rising costs and economic uncertainty" facing American families, but financial records show she collected a combined salary of nearly $250,000 in 2024 and holds an extensive investment portfolio with assets potentially worth nearly $1.8 million and no reportable liabilities. In New Mexico, Rep. Gabe Vasquez, D-N.M., has said he "never had the luxury of financial wealth," argued voters are drawn to candidates who do not "come from wealth," and described his mother as working long hours in Mexico’s "maquiladora industry" to make ends meet. But records reviewed by Fox News Digital show his mother held corporate finance roles at GE, including as a finance manager and comptroller in Mexico and later as a senior finance analyst in Indiana, while social media screenshots shared with Fox News Digital show repeated European travel, luxury shopping and other upscale family photos. DEM IN KEY SWING RACE MISSED NEARLY HALF HER STATE HOUSE VOTES WHILE TAKING TAXPAYER SALARY: 'NO SHOW' Meanwhile, in Washington State, Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, D-Wash., has built part of her blue-collar image around her time working in an auto shop and her Reed College history, saying she worked three jobs and paid for the private liberal arts school "by the credit hour" after her parents stopped paying tuition. But financial disclosures reviewed by Fox News Digital did not list reportable student-loan debt, while critics familiar with her time at Reed College have questioned whether jobs Gluesenkamp Perez cited, including as a nanny, campus barista and at an "iPhone case factory," could have plausibly covered the school’s cost. "Voters can see through the phony double-talk easier than politicians ever realize. It’s far better to be who you are and offer a compelling vision to make voters’ lives better than contort your own biography and background into something it’s not," Republican strategist Colin Reed told Fox News Digital. "Under normal circumstances, financial success and upward mobility would be attributes to lean into as selling points on the campaign trail. But with socialism ascendant and the demonization of wealth not far behind, these are far from normal times." DEMOCRATS CAUGHT ON CAMERA COACHING CANDIDATE ON HOW TO BE 'AUTHENTIC' IN 2026 MESSAGING Bennett, who is running in New Jersey’s competitive 7th Congressional District, disclosed dozens of investments, retirement accounts and other assets in an amended candidate financial disclosure filed with the House on May 15 and reviewed by Fox News Digital. Based on the value ranges listed in the disclosure, her reported assets could be worth as much as roughly $1.8 million. The filing listed no reportable liabilities. Among the holdings were three valued between $50,001 and $100,000 apiece and 17 more valued between $15,001 and $50,000. Because the disclosure reports assets in broad value ranges rather than exact amounts, Bennett’s reported holdings total roughly $447,000 at the low end and nearly $1.8 million at the high end. Using the midpoint of each disclosed range puts their estimated value at roughly $1.12 million.  The disclosure also showed that Bennett received nearly $200,000 in salary from Noom in 2024 and nearly $46,000 from Oshi Health that year, for more than $242,000 combined. The financial picture contrasts with the economic message Bennett has emphasized on the campaign trail, where she has repeatedly invoked her own family's finances and experience as a mother of two. In a June 18 campaign post titled "My 2010 Honda Accord," Bennett said she and her husband still drove the 16-year-old car because "it’s what we can afford," arguing Washington needs more "regular people" who understand families’ financial pressures firsthand. In the post, Bennett specifically pointed to childcare, writing, "I know what it’s like to worry about childcare costs," while also citing rising grocery bills and difficult financial decisions because there is not "an unlimited amount of money sitting in the bank account." Months earlier, she similarly said she was, "like so many of you," navigating the "astronomical" costs of food, education, childcare and healthcare. Those comments also come as FEC records show Bennett’s campaign has paid $21,250 since June 2025 to cover her childcare expenses. Federal election rules permit campaign funds to cover a candidate’s childcare expenses when they are incurred as a direct result of campaign activity. "After serving our country for 15 years as a Navy helicopter pilot, Rebecca swapped her MH-60 Seahawk for the 2010 Honda Accord she uses to drop off her two young children at day care and public school. Rebecca knows firsthand how much childcare costs, and it’s critical that we have people in Congress that understand the challenges New Jersey families are facing," campaign spokesperson Carly Jones told Fox News Digital. "While Tom Kean Jr. plays the stock market in Congress, Rebecca is going to fight to lower costs and end Washington corruption." Meanwhile, Vasquez has also been explicit in casting his background in working-class and blue-collar terms. In his first House floor speech in March 2023, the New Mexico Democrat said, "I’ve never had the luxury of financial wealth," and during his 2022 campaign argued that voters were drawn to a candidate who "doesn’t come from wealth" or money. DSA CO-CHAIR STRUGGLES TO EXPLAIN MILLIONAIRE TAX POLICY Vasquez has also repeatedly pointed to his mother’s work in Mexico’s "maquiladora industry" as part of his family’s working-class story. In an October 2025 La Opinión op-ed, he wrote that his mother, Hortencia Banuelos, "worked long hours in the maquiladora industry working to make ends meet," describing her story as one of "sacrifice, resilience, and hope." In a 2023 interview, Vasquez similarly said his parents worked in the maquiladora industry, including assembling aerospace parts and building sensors for refrigerators and washing machines in Ciudad Juárez. But Banuelos’ own professional profile and other publicly available records reviewed by Fox News Digital show she held senior finance roles at GE during much of Vasquez’s childhood. Her LinkedIn profile lists her as a "Finance Manager/Comptroller" for GE in Mexico from December 1985 to March 1994, overseeing accounting, finance, payroll, accounts payable, IT and customs. She was promoted in 1994 to senior finance analyst at a GE operation in Bloomington, Indiana, where the profile says she analyzed a manufacturing plant with $800 million in revenue and 3,000 employees. A 2020 profile of Banuelos in Hispanic Executive separately reported that GE hired her in Mexico in the 1980s and selected her for a two-year training program geared almost exclusively toward Ivy League graduates before she later moved to Indiana. The professional record is also accompanied by social media material showing a more affluent family lifestyle. Posts from Banuelos’ Facebook and Instagram accounts, screenshots of which were shared and reviewed by Fox News Digital, showed repeated European travel, including a three-month stay in France, while other posts showed Banuelos and Vasquez’s sister shopping at luxury brands. Several photos from upscale locations also included Vasquez himself, including one in which he posed with a Corvette. Vasquez has faced scrutiny over a lavish 2018 ceremony he held with a former fiancée at Akiin Beach Tulum in Mexico as well. The Daily Mail reported in June that events at the beachfront wedding venue can cost between $30,000 and $90,000. Vasquez’s campaign told the outlet that the pair "participated in a private commitment ceremony but were never legally married and eventually separated." DAN BONGINO CALLS SOCIALISM 'BUMPER STICKER POLITICS' AS IT SURGES IN POPULARITY AMONG YOUTH Asked about Vasquez’s characterization of his family background and his mother’s professional record, campaign manager Patricia Socarras Santiago defended Banuelos’ story. "It’s pathetic that as Americans face Trump’s disastrous economy, Republicans attack Gabe’s mom who has worked incredibly hard, starting from the maquiladoras in Mexico, in pursuit of her American Dream," Socarras Santiago told Fox News Digital. "Gabe is incredibly proud of his mom and will work to ensure everyone can access the American Dream and reverse the impacts of Trump’s tanking economy." Gluesenkamp Perez has similarly made her own financial struggles and experience in the trades central to her political biography. In a 2023 interview with Reed Magazine, her alma mater's alumni publication, she said her parents stopped paying her tuition after she stopped attending church.  "Afterwards, I worked three jobs and paid for Reed by the credit hour," Gluesenkamp Perez said, identifying the jobs as working as a nanny, a barista and "in an iPhone case factory." Reed’s own historical records show tuition was $39,440 for the 2010-2011 academic year, with a per-credit tuition charge of $1,625, before rising to $40,940 and $1,750 per credit the following year.  Meanwhile, Gluesenkamp Perez’s latest House financial disclosure, filed May 15, lists two commercial-property notes and a mortgage on her residence but no reportable student-loan debt. Additionally, some of Gluesenkamp Perez’s former Reed classmates have publicly questioned her account of paying for the private college through those jobs. On a Jan. 29 episode of the NOEXIST INC podcast titled "Absolutely Sweet Marie Gluesenkamp Perez," former roommate Isaac Eger said the "iPhone case factory" was actually Grove, now Grovemade, a small Portland company that made bamboo iPhone cases by hand, and recalled that Gluesenkamp Perez did not begin working there until around 2010 or 2011, late in her time at Reed. He also noted the factory was closer to a small handmade bamboo case business that made its products by hand. Eger added on the podcast that Gluesenkamp Perez worked as a barista at Reed’s on-campus Paradox coffee shop and recalled that she did not begin that job until around her senior year. paragraphs: Several battleground Democrats running in competitive House races have leaned on working-class, blue-collar biographies to connect with voters’ economic anxieties, but financial records and other materials reviewed by Fox News Digital complicate the images they have presented on the campaign trail. In New Jersey, for example, Democratic Party candidate Rebecca Bennett has pitched herself as a parent with firsthand understanding of the "rising costs and economic uncertainty" facing American families, but financial records show she collected a combined salary of nearly $250,000 in 2024 and holds an extensive investment portfolio with assets potentially worth nearly $1.8 million and no reportable liabilities. In New Mexico, Rep. Gabe Vasquez, D-N.M., has said he "never had the luxury of financial wealth," argued voters are drawn to candidates who do not "come from wealth," and described his mother as working long hours in Mexico’s "maquiladora industry" to make ends meet. But records reviewed by Fox News Digital show his mother held corporate finance roles at GE, including as a finance manager and comptroller in Mexico and later as a senior finance analyst in Indiana, while social media screenshots shared with Fox News Digital show repeated European travel, luxury shopping and other upscale family photos. "Voters can see through the phony double-talk easier than politicians ever realize. It’s far better to be who you are and offer a compelling vision to make voters’ lives better than contort your own biography and background into something it’s not," Republican strategist Colin Reed told Fox News Digital. "Under normal circumstances, financial success and upward mobility would be attributes to lean into as selling points on the campaign trail. But with socialism ascendant and the demonization of wealth not far behind, these are far from normal times." DEMOCRATS CAUGHT ON CAMERA COACHING CANDIDATE ON HOW TO BE 'AUTHENTIC' IN 2026 MESSAGING Bennett, who is running in New Jersey’s competitive 7th Congressional District, disclosed dozens of investments, retirement accounts and other assets in an amended candidate financial disclosure filed with the House on May 15 and reviewed by Fox News Digital. Based on the value ranges listed in the disclosure, her reported assets could be worth as much as roughly $1.8 million. The filing listed no reportable liabilities. Among the holdings were three valued between $50,001 and $100,000 apiece and 17 more valued between $15,001 and $50,000. Because the disclosure reports assets in broad value ranges rather than exact amounts, Bennett’s reported holdings total roughly $447,000 at the low end and nearly $1.8 million at the high end. Using the midpoint of each disclosed range puts their estimated value at roughly $1.12 million.  The disclosure also showed that Bennett received nearly $200,000 in salary from Noom in 2024 and nearly $46,000 from Oshi Health that year, for more than $242,000 combined. The financial picture contrasts with the economic message Bennett has emphasized on the campaign trail, where she has repeatedly invoked her own family's finances and experience as a mother of two. In a June 18 campaign post titled "My 2010 Honda Accord," Bennett said she and her husband still drove the 16-year-old car because "it’s what we can afford," arguing Washington needs more "regular people" who understand families’ financial pressures firsthand. In the post, Bennett specifically pointed to childcare, writing, "I know what it’s like to worry about childcare costs," while also citing rising grocery bills and difficult financial decisions because there is not "an unlimited amount of money sitting in the bank account." Months earlier, she similarly said she was, "like so many of you," navigating the "astronomical" costs of food, education, childcare and healthcare. Those comments also come as FEC records show Bennett’s campaign has paid $21,250 since June 2025 to cover her childcare expenses. Federal election rules permit campaign funds to cover a candidate’s childcare expenses when they are incurred as a direct result of campaign activity. "After serving our country for 15 years as a Navy helicopter pilot, Rebecca swapped her MH-60 Seahawk for the 2010 Honda Accord she uses to drop off her two young children at day care and public school. Rebecca knows firsthand how much childcare costs, and it’s critical that we have people in Congress that understand the challenges New Jersey families are facing," campaign spokesperson Carly Jones told Fox News Digital. "While Tom Kean Jr. plays the stock market in Congress, Rebecca is going to fight to lower costs and end Washington corruption." Meanwhile, Vasquez has also been explicit in casting his background in working-class and blue-collar terms. In his first House floor speech in March 2023, the New Mexico Democrat said, "I’ve never had the luxury of financial wealth," and during his 2022 campaign argued that voters were drawn to a candidate who "doesn’t come from wealth" or money.
