articles.title: 'Not 1984': Flock cameras watching millions of Americans spark bipartisan revolt
articles.summary: Flock Safety's automatic license plate readers face bipartisan backlash as lawmakers warn AI-powered cameras threaten Fourth Amendment privacy rights.
articles.body: There's a new frontier in the national privacy debate that's uniting people on the right and left, and it's a tool that millions of Americans encounter every day without even realizing it. Automatic license plate reader (ALPR) companies have been brought under scrutiny by lawmakers in Washington as privacy hawks warn that the growing sophistication of artificial intelligence (AI) technology is testing the bounds of what ALPR devices can legally learn about drivers on the road. One company in particular, Flock Safety, has been taking hits in the media and political sphere as news of Flock cameras' misuse — and occasional success — dominates headlines. "There's cameras everywhere, people know that, but if law enforcement has the ability to monitor the comings and goings of citizens, I think that's wrong. I mean, we're not the CCP, we're not 1984 and an Orwellian society, and Americans have rights," Rep. Greg Steube, R-Fla., told Fox News Digital. LICENSE PLATE CAMERAS ARE TRACKING DRIVERS EVERYWHERE He pointed to a recent incident in his district where a now-former Sarasota police officer was fired and arrested after being accused of misusing Flock camera technology, using it to spy on one particular license plate over 300 times. FLOCK SAFETY CAMERAS NEED CONSTITUTIONAL GUARDRAILS BEFORE FURTHER DEPLOYMENT, TENNESSEE MAYOR ARGUES "I don't think you're gonna be able to stop these cameras from being out there, but at the very least, there should be some type of legal parameters put in place to protect people's Fourth Amendment rights," he said. ALPRs automatically capture and analyze vehicle and location data on public roads without drivers' consent. Supporters have argued that it's a critical tool for public safety that only collects minimal information, while opponents labeled it an alarming expansion of the mass surveillance state. LICENSE PLATE CAMERAS AT HOME DEPOT AND LOWE’S SPARK PRIVACY FEARS Rep. Keith Self, R-Texas, told Fox News Digital, "These cameras are well beyond an automated license plate reader today. AI has made them so capable that they are now capable of facial recognition, of seeing what you’re doing inside your car. So it’s well beyond the license plate reader…that’s the problem. Technology has moved these beyond just looking at the back of a car." On the other side of the aisle, a spokesperson for progressive Rep. Delia Ramirez, D-Ill., pointed Fox News Digital to her recent comments responding to news that Flock was updating its oversight standards. Ramirez wrote on X, "Private tech companies have amassed record-breaking profits off our pain and the use of technology for mass surveillance is a threat to our democracy, civil liberties, and privacy. Congress must stop the ever-expanding surveillance state." ‘DARTH VADER’ USES DARK SIDE TO MOCK CONTROVERSIAL SURVEILLANCE CAMERAS: 'THE EMPEROR IS A FAN OF FLOCK' The debate even exploded onto the campaign trail ahead of November's midterm elections, where ALPRs join AI data centers as Big Tech's big boogeymen. "I oppose Flock’s mass surveillance technology, and I’ll stand with anyone in Congress, regardless of party, who wants to put limits on unchecked mass surveillance on the American people," Will Lawrence, a Democrat running for the House in Michigan's 7th Congressional District, told Fox News Digital. DSA CANDIDATE PUSHES FEDERAL AI DATA CENTER MORATORIUM WITH MICHIGAN EARLY VOTING UNDERWAY Abdul El-Sayed, the insurgent progressive Democratic nominee for Senate in Michigan, accused his opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers, R-Mich., of supporting Flock cameras in a campaign video released on X. "There's been this mass proliferation of black cameras, any and everywhere, little cameras, watching your every move to collect information about you without you even noticing," he said in the video. "If you believe, like me, that you shouldn't just be surveilled because you're driving along the street, then I hope I can earn your support." A spokesperson for Rogers told Fox News Digital that he "vehemently opposes unchecked use of Flock cameras to track law-abiding citizens. Security and liberty aren’t enemies. Good government protects both." Back on Capitol Hill, the furor over these cameras has prompted a flurry of legislative pushback. Self is among the House lawmakers pushing bills aimed at the issue, along with Reps. Tim Burchett, R-Tenn., and Thomas Massie, R-Ky. Steube told Fox News Digital that he's also "looking at filing something at the national level," and is sending a letter to Sarasota, Florida, officials threatening to withhold federal funding absent a promise of "reasonable restrictions" to "prevent the abuses that have happened right here in our backyard." Privacy and misuse concerns have sparked efforts across the country to cut ties with Flock specifically, from Lansing, Michigan, to Bernadillo County, New Mexico. Flock is just one company of several that operate ALPRs, some of which have been used for years. But the technology does have its benefits and has been used to stop crime. Flock Safety founder and CEO Garrett Langley told Fox News' "Saturday in America" that his technology has helped police find missing children at least twice, including after a recent carjacking in Atlanta. Flock has also said it does not use facial recognition and recently introduced new safety controls in response to the public backlash. "When I think about legislation that calls for an outright ban, that's like banning vehicles. That would never have made sense. Instead, what we did is we introduced laws against drunk driving. We introduced laws around seatbelts, laws around airbags," Langley said. "What happens if law enforcement abuses this powerful technology today? It is too often that in Flock and in other technologies, there's no regulation, there's no accountability. And we think that's wrong." Supporters of ALPRs like Flock cameras have held them up as a key crime-fighting tool, while agreeing that guardrails to prevent abuse would be helpful. "I think it's definitely a net positive. And I think that's a very easy call... the use cases and the documented cases of these things being effective tools, I think, vastly outnumber the handful of cases of abuse and misuse that we've seen," Rafael Mangual, a senior fellow at the Manhattan Institute, told Fox News Digital. "The fact that some police officers will misuse their firearms, for example, to hurt people, is not a reason to take away all police officers' firearms." Mangual said he disagreed with accusations of Fourth Amendment violations as well: "I think as of right now, these cameras can't be used to do the sorts of things that courts have recognized require a warrant." Jim Pasco, executive director of the National Fraternal Order of Police, told Fox News Digital, "There’s an awful lot of new and still developing technology out there that's very helpful to law enforcement and to enhancing public safety. That said, all of these systems need to be regulated to ensure that they aren't abused." He also cautioned against making policy decisions in the heat of an election cycle. "The most dangerous time of governance to have a crisis in is an even-numbered year, because elections are always held in even-numbered years. And I would say this problem and this year are no exception," Pasco said. "There needs to be a very careful analysis of the benefits and the risks inherent in abuse and any action that's taken should, if anything, enhance the potential for these systems being used for good and minimize the chances of abuse." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Let's not throw out the baby with the bath water here."

articles.title: DOJ sues to stop Ohio court blocking courthouse arrests
articles.summary: DOJ sues to stop Ohio court blocking courthouse arrests
articles.body: The Justice Department sued an Ohio court Tuesday over a new rule blocking federal immigration arrests at or near the courthouse, accusing local officials of unlawfully interfering with federal enforcement and forcing ICE agents to make arrests in potentially riskier settings. At issue is a Franklin County Municipal Court rule, which bars civil arrests at the courthouse unless officers have a judicial warrant. The DOJ argues the rule conflicts with federal immigration law, which allows ICE agents in certain circumstances to make arrests with administrative warrants or no warrant at all. "This type of rule obstructs federal law enforcement and facilitates evasion of federal law by dangerous criminal aliens, despite Congress’s direction that federal agents detain and remove them," said Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate of the Justice Department’s Civil Division. "Throughout the country, and including in this courthouse specifically, federal agents have routinely and safely conducted arrests. The Department of Justice is committed to protecting that important federal prerogative." This is a developing news story; check back for updates.

articles.title: Trump administration says it might demolish the Kennedy Center if court blocks renovations
articles.summary: Justice Department attorneys called the Kennedy Center “structurally unsound, fundamentally unsafe, and embarrassing to the Nation’s Capital.”
articles.body: The Trump administration is, for the first time, threatening the demolition of the Kennedy Center if the arts institution isn’t allowed to follow its plans for the site, including adding President Donald Trump’s name to the front of the building. “Without those efforts, the Center will deteriorate further into an unsafe, decrepit structure that will be required to be taken down, with a determination to follow on what to build on the site, such as a large outdoor amphitheater overlooking the Potomac River that has been proposed, by some, for many years,” Justice Department attorney Brantley T. Mayers wrote in a court filing on Monday. The filing notes that any potential outdoor amphitheater would “fail to adequately honor” President John F. Kennedy, “but would be simpler and more economical to build, operate, and maintain.” The DOJ attorneys called the Kennedy Center “structurally unsound, fundamentally unsafe, and embarrassing to the Nation’s Capital.” They said the center’s board, which was handpicked by self-appointed chairman Trump, “recognizes that President Trump’s efforts and prestige provide the sole hope for the Center’s financial survival, and structural renewal.” “The Board also underscores, and the undisputed evidence demonstrates, that without the prominent recognition of The Trump Administration, and President Trump’s efforts, the donors will not contribute, and the Center will continue to be in a financial and structural death spiral. The Trump Administration, and President Donald J. Trump, should, therefore, be given the respect and dignity of acknowledgement,” the filing says. It notes that Trump “obtained $258 million in funding from Congress for capital restoration, and has marshalled a new donor base to finance an endowment for the Center,” but does not say what has happened to that money. The filing makes a dramatic twist in the monthslong saga to renovate the historic arts institution, which has faced multiple legal challenges and criticism from Democrats, musicians and members of the Kennedy family. This language is a shift from what Kennedy Center Executive Director Matt Floca has used in recent months to describe what the board has said are necessary renovations. Floca has said the renovations would include a “total replacement of stage lifts and rigging systems” and wide-ranging electrical work and leak prevention that could be completed within two years if the facility was shut down during the renovations. He said in a court filing earlier this year that the “exterior of the Center’s main building will not be materially affected” and “the planned construction, renovation, and renewal efforts will not tear down the Center to its structural steel.” A spokesperson for the center said Tuesday that the language in the filing “describes a hypothetical scenario of what could happen if the center’s desperately needed renovation is blocked by partisan interests.” A center official had previously said the facility would not be gutted. “You’re not going to be able to stand in Georgetown and look over the river and see through the building,” the official told reporters during a tour of the facility in April. “That’s not what’s going to happen.” Mayers’ filing Monday suggested only Trump and his people could save the arts institution. The administration has “committed an enormous amount of time and energy in planning for the forthcoming renovation and restoration of this building, a task which President Trump, given his unrivaled expertise and experience in real estate and construction, and prominence as President, is uniquely qualified to accomplish,” Mayers wrote Monday in opposition to a motion from Rep. Joyce Beatty, D-Ohio, to block the administration from closing the center completely. “Even Beatty should prefer a healthy, restored Center to a decaying hulk that is doomed to inevitable destruction or collapse. The Court should allow the Board and President Trump to bring the Center back to a level of greatness far higher than it has ever had before. This would be the fitting tribute that President Kennedy so well deserves.” Beatty has claimed the closure decision was rushed and that board members weren’t presented with enough information about various scenarios before having to vote on it. The congresswoman did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the DOJ filing. She is challenging the Trump-appointed board’s renewed bid to add Trump’s name to the front of the building. A judge found the board’s earlier bid to do so was unlawful and compelled it to remove the president’s name from the building, which is supposed to be a “living memorial” to the slain president. Trump is appealing and the board voted this month to add his name back to the building in a slightly different way- going from the since-stricken “The Donald J. Trump and John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts” to “The John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump.” There is a hearing scheduled on the planned name change and closure in D.C. on Thursday afternoon. The judge said in his earlier decision that only Congress has the power to rename the site.

articles.title: GOP's Singer 'very prepared' to oust Dem Moskowitz in toss-up Florida race that could determine House majority
articles.summary: Scott Singer says Florida's redrawn 25th Congressional District gives Republicans a path to flip Jared Moskowitz's seat in a narrowly divided House.
articles.body: Rep. Jared Moskowitz, D-Fla., a self-described moderate, is facing political headwinds in the race for the newly-redrawn 25th Congressional District in South Florida, as Republican nominee Scott Singer sees a path to pick up a House seat in a narrowly divided Congress. "We're going to be very prepared to go flip this seat – it is a key targeted seat," Singer told Fox News Digital in an interview Monday. "This is a key district that may determine the balance of power in the House." FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: DEMOCRATS LEAD IN THE HOUSE, BUT REDISTRICTING KEEPS THE GOP IN THE GAME The race is drawing national attention and, potentially, big Democratic dollars to defend the seat in Democrats' pursuit of the majority to attack what House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries just called the "cartel" of President Donald Trump. "A lot of people in this district and beyond understand what's at stake here," Singer, former Boca Raton mayor, said. Moskowitz, currently seated in the more Democratic-friendly 23rd District, is – like Singer – Jewish and pro-Israel, but he will have to navigate a tougher Republican-friendly map and fend off the "anti-Israel wing" of the Democratic Party, according to to Singer. FLORIDA DEMOCRAT SENDS 'CONDOLENCES' TO HASAN PIKER AFTER DEFEATING DSA CHALLENGER IN FLORIDA PRIMARY "His voting record speaks volumes," Singer said. "Since he's gotten to Congress, he's been locked up with the Democrats on almost every issue." "This is not the sort of record of bipartisanship he once had. He's been much more partisan because he has to be," Singer claimed. "He has to appeal to a more far-left socialist led Democratic Party if he's going to have any influence. And that's going home to roost in November." When reached for comment, the two-term Moskowitz stressed he fought of the Democratic Socialists of America's maximum pressure campaign in his primary, while keeping $2 million cash on hand for the general election and expecting "we'll have the national resources" in the fight to keep the seat blue. "I go after my party all the time and fight within," Moskowitz, who was twice appointed to positions by Republican Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis in a show of bipartisanship, told Fox News Digital, noting Singer has been "awfully silent" on social media amid his own vocal defense against the "anti-Israel" political factions. FROM WASSERMAN SCHULTZ TO GOLDMAN, DEMOCRATIC INCUMBENTS ARE FIGHTING FOR SURVIVAL "Scott just has talking points, which is why he's the masked singer. You hear a voice behind a mask. He says things to all sorts of people, tells people what they want to hear, but nobody really knows where he stands because he never really takes positions." The heated rhetoric belies a previously tighter relationship. "Scott Singer endorsed me when I ran the first time," Moskowitz claimed. Singer's campaign has denied it was anything more than a personal call to generally express support for a fellow Jewish, pro-Israel politician. Singer, though, says he is well-positioned in the newly redrawn South Florida district, with a growing GOP voter-registration advantage and Democratic division working against the "quasi-incumbent." "People are abandoning the Democratic Party because the mainstream Democratic Party of even a few years ago has abandoned them," Singer said. "It's now a socialist-led party and it's sad for America." "That's why we need to band together and make sure independent voters understand what's at stake," he added. "We can't have people talking about communism or new Democrat-incoming members of the House saying horrific things like that they would wipe their hand on the American flag if they didn't have a napkin. That's today's Democratic Party, unfortunately, and it's not something I want to see." MOSKOWITZ REJECTS RICK SCOTT'S CLAIMS HE'S 'SCARED TO DEATH' OF SOCIALISTS, BEHOLDEN TO HASAN PIKER The race is considered to be one of 19 toss-ups in the nation (seats held by four Democrats and 15 Republicans), according to the Cook Political Report. "It's now about five points more Republican than Democrat, but even since redistricting, there are Republicans who are registering at a higher rate: People in Florida have seen the success of our state and seen the craziness other places, and they're voting more conservative," Singer said. "And we have a great opportunity to pick off disaffected Democrats who are sick with the socialist lean, especially in our community that has a large number of residents who fled communism, like my family, like wife's family did," he continued. "They understand that bringing socialism and communism into the United States is a terrible idea. That's another reason why we're optimistic about our chances to flip this must-win seat in November." DESANTIS UNDER PRESSURE AS FLORIDA REDRAW COULD TIP HOUSE BALANCE IN GOP MAP FIGHT The race also presents an unusual political dynamic: Singer and Moskowitz are both Jewish candidates competing in a district where roughly a quarter of the electorate is Jewish, one of the highest concentrations in the country. "The anti-Israel wing, which has taken root in the Democratic Party, is doing the convincing for us," Singer said. "Because we've seen a majority of House members would deny arms sales to Israel, our ally during a time of conflict. "And that's the party, where it is. We've seen three incumbents in the Democratic Party ousted in recent months solely because Israel was the key issue. "Anti-Israel is winning. It's become the mainstream of the Democratic Party. And longtime Democrats are leaving in droves. Another reason why it's going to be very hard for Democrats in this district to win with 25% Jewish population and people who understand Israel's close and long-standing alliance with the United States. We're going to pick off more of those voters." 5 TAKEAWAYS FROM FLORIDA SENATE PRIMARY: GOP SEN. ASHLEY MOODY WILL FACE DSA'S NIXON Also, while GOP-leaning, the district is still largely independent. It snakes along South Florida's Atlantic coast through portions of Palm Beach, Broward and Miami-Dade counties, encompassing communities around Delray Beach, Boca Raton, Fort Lauderdale, Hollywood and Miami Beach. "I was already running under the prior boundaries when it leaned Democratic, but I'm thrilled with the new boundaries because it runs from Miami Beach, where I was born, through Fort Lauderdale where I grew up, through Boca Raton where I served as mayor for eight years," Singer said. "I have deep ties in this district. It's my whole life. I've lived 40-plus years in this District in all three counties. My opponent doesn't live in the district. I'm not sure he's ever lived in the district. And I think those community ties help when you're trying to represent 750,000-plus people." Moskowitz lives in nearby Parkland and was born and raised in Coral Springs, which is just west of the newly drawn district, which carved those towns out. FLA DEM SEN-NOMINEE ANGIE NIXON BACKED ABOLISHING ELECTORAL COLLEGE, RANKED-CHOICE VOTING IN RESURFACED CLIPS Trump would have carried the territory by roughly nine points in 2024 after Joe Biden would have won it by about five points in 2020, showing just how the district is turning conservative and more favorable to flip. "Jewish voters don't just have to vote for a Jewish candidate who may be not terrible on Israel ... now you have a pro-Israel, Zionist candidate who's a strong Republican who will vote for the common sense solutions: We need like less regulation, lower taxes, insurance reform and more." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Independent voters have a choice," he added. "Are we going to continue on tax reform, secure borders, economic improvement... or are we going to go back to what the Democrats would propose, which frankly for the next two years is just impeachment? "Nothing will get done in Washington," he concluded.

articles.title: Second lady Usha Vance fires back at pointed jab from Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed
articles.summary: Usha Vance responded to Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed's remark that seemingly questioned whether JD Vance's Papaw would have accepted her Indian ethnicity.
articles.body: PROGRAMMING NOTE: Watch the exclusive interview with second lady Usha Vance Wednesday on "Fox & Friends," starting at 6am ET. Second lady Usha Vance responded to what critics described as a "racist" dig from Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, who appeared to question how Vice President JD Vance’s grandfather would have regarded her. The exchange began after Vance criticized El-Sayed’s views on Sharia law during a rally in Ohio, arguing the practice would be completely alien to his grandfather, whom he calls his "Papaw." "He once argued, not too long ago, that criticisms of Sharia law were rooted in White supremacy," Vance said of El-Sayed, the American-born son of Muslim Egyptian immigrants. VANCE UNLOADS ON EL-SAYED OVER SHARIA REMARKS: ‘THAT’S NOT MY GRANDPA’S DEMOCRATIC PARTY’ "I'd love to go back in time and tell my Papaw that there is a man who claims to stand for working people who says not only should we have Sharia law, but if you criticize it, you're a White supremacist. That's not my Papaw’s Democratic Party, my friends," the vice president continued. Responding to the vice president’s jab, El-Sayed wrote: "So do we think JD is taking Usha with him back in time to meet Papaw, or no…" Critics interpreted the remark as an insinuation that Vance’s grandfather would not have accepted Usha because of her Indian heritage. EL-SAYED UNDER FIRE ONLINE AFTER TAKING AIM AT USHA VANCE, FEMALE TRUMP AIDE IN WEEKEND SOCIAL MEDIA POSTS "I have to admit, I kind of laughed," Usha Vance told "Fox & Friends" in an exclusive interview set to air Wednesday morning. "Because yes, I never met JD's Mamaw and Papaw. But I do know and love the children that they raised, his mom, his aunt and uncle. And they have never been anything but incredibly loving." El-Sayed further addressed the comment in an interview on Saturday. "The confusing thing about it is that he thinks that there are some people who are more American than others because they can point to their Papaw who was here earlier," he told MS NOW. "And my question to him is simply: Why is it then, how do you look your parents-in-law in the eye and say that somehow they're less American than you are? Because that's what he's implying there." JD was raised in large part by his grandparents, James and Bonnie Vance, who he calls his "Papaw" and "Mamaw." James died in 1997 and Bonnie died eight years later. Usha and JD met while attending Yale Law School and married in 2014. Although she never met her husband's late grandparents, the mother of four said her husband’s aunt has become a "second mother" to her. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "His aunt is like a second mother to me," said the second lady. "And so I have to think that if they raised children like that, they would have been loving as well. And I would have really, really, really loved to have met them." In his 2016 memoir, "Hillbilly Elegy," Vance wrote that one of his "great regrets" was that his grandparents never had the opportunity to meet his wife. El-Sayed’s campaign did not return Fox News Digital's request for comment.

articles.title: Mamdani launches fast-track housing-court push, says landlords unable to comply ‘should not be a landlord’
articles.summary: Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced New York City's Unified Court System will fast-track emergency housing court cases involving vacate orders and violations.
articles.body: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced Tuesday the debut of the city's new Unified Court System, a mechanism to fast-track emergency cases in New York City Housing Court. "I am proud to announce that the Unified Court System will now fast-track emergency housing court cases where the health, safety and well-being of New Yorkers is at risk," Mamdani said during a Tuesday news conference. The new system will reduce the time tenants face to have emergency hearings on potential negligence from landlords, Mamdani explained. "This fast track will accelerate the cases that are both the most egregious and the most complex. Cases where at least one third of units in a building are subject to an open vacate order. Where families have been forced from their homes. Cases where at least one third of the units have an open and immediately hazardous violation for essential services," he announced. MANHATTAN BUILDING STABILIZED, SOME EVACUATIONS LIFTED AFTER COLLAPSE FEARED In cases of "persistent and extreme negligence" where tenants request entirely new building management, judges will require parties to return to court "within five days after service is completed," Mamdani announced. NYC RENT BOARD DISSENTER WARNS MAMDANI-BACKED FREEZE COULD HURT AFFORDABLE HOUSING OVER TIME: 'SLOW BURN' When asked how his office would differentiate between a landlord who was persistently negligent and one who simply couldn't afford to keep up with the costs of building management, Mamdani did not hold back. "We're talking about cases where a third of the building is facing some kind of a serious violation. Cases where we have elevators broken down," he started. MAMDANI RIPPED OVER 'FREAK SHOW' NEWS CONFERENCE WHERE EVICTION WAS DECLARED A FORM OF 'VIOLENCE' "When it comes to the law, everyone has to follow it. And for far too long that has somehow not been understood when it comes to housing in our city. If a landlord is not able to follow the law, then they should not be a landlord of that property," he replied. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP When asked about how to enforce any violators who might not appear to Housing Court after the five-day window, Mamdani said "there is still a lot of work to follow through on." Fox News Digital contacted the mayor's office for further comment.

"This fast track will accelerate the cases that are both the most egregious and the most complex. Cases where at least one third of units in a building are subject to an open vacate order. Where families have been forced from their homes. Cases where at least one third of the units have an open and immediately hazardous violation for essential services," he announced. MANHATTAN BUILDING STABILIZED, SOME EVACUATIONS LIFTED AFTER COLLAPSE FEARED In cases of "persistent and extreme negligence" where tenants request entirely new building management, judges will require parties to return to court "within five days after service is completed," Mamdani announced. NYC RENT BOARD DISSENTER WARNS MAMDANI-BACKED FREEZE COULD HURT AFFORDABLE HOUSING OVER TIME: 'SLOW BURN' When asked how his office would differentiate between a landlord who was persistently negligent and one who simply couldn't afford to keep up with the costs of building management, Mamdani did not hold back. "We're talking about cases where a third of the building is facing some kind of a serious violation. Cases where we have elevators broken down," he started. MAMDANI RIPPED OVER 'FREAK SHOW' NEWS CONFERENCE WHERE EVICTION WAS DECLARED A FORM OF 'VIOLENCE' "When it comes to the law, everyone has to follow it. And for far too long that has somehow not been understood when it comes to housing in our city. If a landlord is not able to follow the law, then they should not be a landlord of that property," he replied. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP When asked about how to enforce any violators who might not appear to Housing Court after the five-day window, Mamdani said "there is still a lot of work to follow through on." Fox News Digital contacted the mayor's office for further comment.

articles.title: Trump mourns Dolly Parton, orders US flags lowered nationwide after country music icon dies
articles.summary: Trump ordered American flags lowered nationwide for one week in honor of Dolly Parton, calling her death "a true loss for millions of people."
articles.body: President Donald Trump ordered American flags lowered across the United States for one week Tuesday, as he mourned the death of country music icon Dolly Parton, telling the legendary singer, "The World loves you." Parton died peacefully Tuesday in Nashville, Tennessee, according to an announcement shared by her representatives. She was 80. "Very sad to report that Dolly Parton, one of the greatest Country singers, and far beyond, EVER, has just passed away," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "This is a true loss for millions of people. There has never been anyone like her, and never will." DOLLY PARTON’S ONGOING HEALTH BATTLE FORCES COUNTRY LEGEND TO MISS MAJOR DOLLYWOOD EVENT Trump then announced a presidential tribute to Parton. "In her honor, I am lowering the American flag throughout the United States for a one week period beginning tonight at 6:00PM," Trump wrote. "Rest in Peace, Dolly! The World loves you." Trump's tribute came as Parton's family and representatives remembered a woman whose influence stretched far beyond the country music stages that made her famous. "A rhinestone life that shone bright enough for the world to see, Dolly will forever stand as an inspiration not only through her timeless music and prolific songwriting, but also her wit, warmth, and kindness that made us all feel like family," the announcement said. "Dolly Parton’s legacy is one of love, compassion, and resilience." DOLLY PARTON CANCELS LAS VEGAS RESIDENCY AS HEALTH ISSUES FORCE HER TO STEP BACK FROM STAGE PERFORMANCES Parton, born Jan. 19, 1946, had a seven-decade career spanning music, songwriting, acting, writing and philanthropy. She was preceded in death by her husband of 59 years, Carl Thomas Dean, who died in 2025, as well as her mother, Avie Lee Caroline Owens, and father, Robert Lee Parton Sr., according to the announcement. DOLLY PARTON'S CALIFORNIA RETREAT WITH WIG ROOM AND DOLLYWOOD BIRDHOUSE LISTS FOR $1.95M At Parton's request, a small, private service will be held for immediate family. Fans and friends were encouraged to pay tribute on social media or through Parton's official website. In lieu of flowers, the family asked for donations to Dolly Parton's Imagination Library. TAYLOR SWIFT'S VIDEO TRIBUTE TO ALAN JACKSON DIVIDES CROWD AT COUNTRY LEGEND'S FINAL SHOW Parton's nephew and head of security, Bryan Seaver, also shared a video message following her death. Tributes quickly poured in from Tennessee and across the country. CARRIE UNDERWOOD, GARY SINISE LEAD STARS WHO'VE SHARED WHY THEY'RE PROUD TO BE AMERICANS "There are no words to adequately express the sorrow our family and indeed, all Tennesseans, feel in the loss of Dolly Parton," Sen. Marsha Blackburn, R-Tenn., wrote on X. "An iconic leader who loved our great state and nation. Her passing leaves a void that no one can ever fill. Dolly, we will always love you." House Republicans called Parton "an American icon" and "a national treasure," praising her as "a legendary artist, a generous philanthropist, and a proud daughter of Tennessee whose music and spirit touched generations of Americans." SEN. LINDSEY GRAHAM DEAD AT 71 AFTER 'BRIEF AND SUDDEN' ILLNESS, OFFICE SAYS Rep. Tim Burchett, R-Tenn., remembered Parton as "an incredible East Tennessean" who "never changed her accent or forgot where she came from." Texas Gov. Greg Abbott announced his state would also lower its flags in Parton's honor. "So sad to lose this legend," Abbott wrote on X. "Texas will lower our flags in her honor. God Bless Dolly." House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., said "America has lost a true national treasure," pointing to Parton's Tennessee roots, worldwide success and philanthropy. "Dolly Parton’s unmistakable voice, joyful spirit, and remarkable generosity touched generations of Americans and many others around the world," Johnson wrote. "From the mountains of Tennessee to stages across the globe, she never forgot where she came from, and she used her extraordinary success to lift up countless others." The Department of the Interior paid tribute to Parton's deep connection to her Tennessee roots and the Great Smoky Mountains. "Dolly Parton carried the music, stories and spirit of her Tennessee mountain home wherever she went," the department said. "She was a lifelong champion of the Great Smoky Mountains and proudly shared her love for them with the world." The Franklin Police Department also mourned the singer, saying her "roots and heart were always deeply connected to Tennessee." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Parton's family said the music and generosity that defined her extraordinary life would endure. "Her songs will continue to resonate with people of all ages," the announcement said, "and her philanthropic work will have a lasting impact."

articles.title: Georgia redistricting battle revived after appeals court overturns federal court decision
articles.summary: The 11th Circuit said Georgia’s 2021 redistricting maps must be reevaluated under the Supreme Court’s newly clarified racial-discrimination standard.
articles.body: Georgia secured a major victory Tuesday in its long-running redistricting battle after a federal appeals court overturned a lower court ruling that the state’s 2021 maps violated the Voting Rights Act, sending the case back for a complete re-evaluation. The 11th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals said the lower court must determine whether there was a "strong inference" that the maps were intentionally drawn to dilute Black voting power, rather than simply finding that the maps had a discriminatory effect under permissible partisan gerrymandering. The decision follows a major Supreme Court ruling in a similar Louisiana case that significantly modified the legal framework for determining racial discrimination in redistricting. The high court said plaintiffs must provide evidence of "present-day intentional racial discrimination." "Plaintiffs must be able to show that voters are engaged in racial-bloc voting because of race, not partisan affiliation," the ruling stated. BLOCKBUSTER SUPREME COURT VOTING RIGHTS RULING IGNITES REDISTRICTING WAR ACROSS SOUTHERN STATES In 2023, a federal judge ruled that Georgia’s congressional and state legislative maps drawn after the 2020 census violated Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act and issued a permanent injunction barring Georgia from using the maps in future elections. The lower court specifically ordered the state to create additional majority-Black districts across the state Senate, state House of Representatives and U.S. congressional districts. Meanwhile, a similar redistricting battle was unfolding in Louisiana, where Robinson v. Ardoin challenged the state’s congressional map, which initially included just one majority-Black district out of six. FEDERAL JUDGE BLOCKS ALABAMA REDISTRICTING PLAN IN BLOW TO TRUMP A federal court later ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, ordering Louisiana to create a second majority-Black district after finding that the original map violated the Voting Rights Act. However, a group of non-minority voters later challenged the new map, arguing that the newly created district amounted to racial gerrymandering and violated the 14th and 15th Amendments. In the second lawsuit, Louisiana v. Callais, the Supreme Court ultimately upheld the constitutionality of Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act while clarifying how courts should evaluate claims of racial discrimination in redistricting. The ruling emphasized the need for evidence supporting a "strong inference" of intentional discrimination, rather than relying solely on the effects of a map. WHY THE SUPREME COURT GUTTED THE VOTING RIGHTS ACT AFTER SIX DECADES IN A BLOW TO BLACK POLITICIANS The decision also altered the legal framework federal courts have used for decades to evaluate racial vote-dilution claims. Established in the Supreme Court’s 1986 ruling in Thornburg v. Gingles, the Gingles framework generally did not require plaintiffs to prove that lawmakers acted with racial intent and instead focused on whether a voting system had discriminatory effects. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Georgia case will now return to the district court for reconsideration under the Supreme Court’s framework established in Louisiana v. Callais.

articles.title: Newsom promises new legal fight after Trump gets Supreme Court victory on mail-in voting
articles.summary: California Gov. Gavin Newsom says the state will sue again after the Supreme Court's 6-3 ruling allowed Trump's mail-in voting restrictions.
articles.body: California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced plans to sue the Trump administration over its push to restrict mail-in voting after the Supreme Court allowed the administration to enforce challenged provisions of President Donald Trump’s executive order for "election integrity" while litigation continues. The announcement sets up the next phase of the legal fight after the Supreme Court (SCOTUS) ruled 6-3 in favor of the Trump administration Monday, lifting an injunction that had blocked the order in 23 states ahead of November's midterm elections. SCOTUS stressed that its decision addressed the injunction rather than the ultimate legality of the order, leaving the door open to additional challenges. Newsom criticized the decision in a statement released by his office. JACKSON RIPS INTO SUPREME COURT COLLEAGUES' 'SERIOUS LEGAL ERROR' ON TRUMP MAIL-IN VOTING ORDER "The Supreme Court just let the Trump administration move ahead (for now) with its plan to disenfranchise voters across the country," Newsom said. "California will be suing AGAIN to block these Orwellian rules from being implemented." Newsom’s office also highlighted two election-related bills moving through the California Legislature that the governor says would protect the state’s elections from interference. According to the governor’s office, AB 282 would establish new felonies involving the seizure of ballots, election records or certified voting technology before election results are certified. SB 259 would establish criminal penalties for interfering with the delivery or return of mail-in ballots, including a felony carrying up to four years in prison in certain cases. CALIFORNIA ACCUSED OF BLOCKING FEDERAL VOTER ROLL AUDIT AS DOJ ESCALATES PROBE OF ELECTION FRAUD CLAIMS The governor’s office described the measures as an "Election Protection" package and said they build on election-related legislation Newsom signed earlier this summer. The U.S. Postal Service (USPS) and Department of Justice said they would move to implement the revised mail-ballot restrictions following Monday’s ruling. Trump’s executive order directs federal agencies to compile citizenship-based lists of eligible voters and directs the USPS to deliver mail-in ballots only to people appearing on approved lists. USPS WOULDN'T DELIVER BALLOTS IN STATES THAT REFUSE TO FORK OVER MAIL-IN VOTER INFO UNDER PROPOSED RULE In explaining its decision, the Supreme Court concluded that the challenged provision directing the Department of Homeland Security to create and distribute state citizenship lists imposed obligations on federal agencies rather than the states themselves. The court wrote: "[It] directs the Secretary of Homeland Security to take appropriate action to create and distribute State Citizenship Lists. This provision is an internal directive from the President to a subordinate. It imposes no obligations on the States, so they ‘suffer no concrete harm from’ it, and without concrete harm, there is no standing." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson dissented. A representative for Newsom did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

articles.title: Democrats see an opening in Texas. Is it déjà vu or a breakthrough?: From the Politics Desk
articles.summary: In today’s edition, Natasha Korecki breaks down the Democratic and the Republican theory of the case in the Texas Senate race.
articles.body: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail. In today’s edition, Natasha Korecki breaks down the Democratic and the Republican theory of the case in the Texas Senate race. Plus, we lay out what to watch for in tonight’s elections. Sign up to receive this newsletter in your inbox every weekday here. — Adam Wollner Democrats see an opening in Texas. Is it déjà vu or a breakthrough? Analysis by Natasha Korecki Texas Democrats have been here before. Their Senate candidate has shot to national prominence, raised gobs of money and is within striking distance of the Republican in the polls. In 2018, that was Beto O’Rourke, who ultimately lost narrowly to GOP Sen. Ted Cruz. Today, it’s James Talarico, who’s up against state Attorney General Ken Paxton. This time, it seems Democrats have learned their lesson about getting too bullish too soon. Even privately, they typically sum up their chances in Texas cautiously, saying it’s the best chance they’ve had in years. It’s been some 30 years since a Democrat has won statewide in Texas. At the same time, the race appears competitive enough that each party considers Texas a battleground this fall, forcing Republicans to spend in and defend in what typically is safe territory. “We have it in our top-tier states,” said Lauren French, the communications director for Senate Majority PAC, a super PAC with ties to Senate Democratic leadership. That list includes Maine, Michigan, Georgia, North Carolina, Alaska, Iowa and Ohio. Here’s what Democrats say they have going for them that could make this year different. Candidate quality: Talarico is a gifted speaker and a seminarian, who attempts to tap into his Christian faith to attract unlikely supporters. Meanwhile, Paxton brings some personal baggage to the race. He was impeached by the state House in 2023 — including 70% of the chamber’s Republicans — only to be acquitted in the state Senate. In addition, Paxton’s wife cited “biblical grounds” when she filed for divorce last year. Fundraising: Talarico has quickly catapulted to one of the top fundraisers in the party. Since 2025, he has brought in $72 million, compared to Paxton’s $16.8 million. That gives him the benefit of paying cheaper ad rates than outside groups and having plenty of runway to reserve TV air time. Environment and demographics. While President Donald Trump remains popular with the GOP base in Texas, Democrats say they see two vital groups moving away from him: Hispanic voters and independents. And here’s what Republicans say Paxton has going for him. Outside money: While Talarico has the edge in candidate fundraising, the cavalry is coming to help Paxton. Tech billionaire Elon Musk is reportedly planning to pour millions of dollars into the Texas Senate race alone. And on Thursday, Trump is slated to head a Republican National Committee fundraiser in Houston that’s aimed at benefiting the state party. Culture wars: Talarico has walked back some of the “cringey comments” he made in the past, including saying God is “nonbinary.” Expect Republicans to elevate these sort of remarks, as well as what Bernadette Breslin, the national press secretary for the National Republican Senatorial Committee, referred to as “climate alarmism.” “The problem for the Democrats excited about James Talarico is the things they like about him … make him unelectable in a Texas general election,” Breslin added. Structural advantage: It’s still Texas, which has served as a Republican stronghold for decades. “We’re feeling really confident. … Texas is one of those states that Democrats try to make really competitive,” said RNC national press secretary Natalie Baldassarre. But then reality of the state’s Republican leaning hits, she added. As for polls showing Talarico close? “As soon as the negative ads start flying, I think they’ll dip from there,” she said. Trump’s endorsement faces major tests in tonight’s primary runoffs By Ben Kamisar and Bridget Bowman Primary season may be starting to slow down, but there are still a couple of notable runoffs in South Carolina and Oklahoma tonight that will test President Donald Trump’s influence over the GOP amid a shaky August for his preferred candidates. Here are the races to watch. South Carolina Senate: Trump has expended significant political capital to boost appointed Sen. Darline Graham in this race. He appeared in the state last week for a rally, held a tele-rally last night, and his allied super PAC has spent $830,000 on texts and phone calls to voters. Graham is facing off against Rep. Ralph Norman in a primary runoff to replace her late brother on the November ballot. As Steve Kornacki notes in his “Data Dive” newsletter, Graham led 33% to 25% in the first round of voting earlier this month and finished ahead of Norman in 36 of the state’s 46 counties. But she has faced renewed scrutiny over her lack of experience in the final stretch of the campaign. Oklahoma governor: Trump also waded in here, with former state Sen. Mike Mazzei leaning heavily into the president’s endorsement as he seeks to succeed term-limited Republican Gov. Kevin Stitt. Mazzei narrowly finished second to state Attorney General Gentner Drummond in the initial June primary. Drummond has been embracing the president too: His website prominently features a photograph of him standing alongside Trump. But Trump has taken to social media in recent days to pan Drummond as a “fake Republican.” Oklahoma Senate: Even ruby red Oklahoma is hosting an ideological and generational Democratic clash. The leading vote-getter in the initial Democratic Senate primary was 31-year-old N’Kiyla Jasmine Thomas, who identifies as a democratic socialist. She’s facing 70-year-old Jim Priest, a moderate attorney and minister. Either would be a heavy underdog against Republican Rep. Kevin Hern in November. Georgia’s 13th District: There’s also a special election to serve the remainder of Rep. David Scott’s term. The race is between two Democrats: Marcye Scott, the late congressman’s daughter, and former Gwinnett County School Board Chairman Everton Blair. Scott led Blair in the preliminary primary 46% to 37%. Read more → 🎥 Tune in to the Kornacki Cam at 7 p.m. ET to watch Steve break down tonight’s results. That’s all From the Politics Desk for now. Today’s newsletter was compiled by Adam Wollner. If you have feedback — likes or dislikes — email us at politicsnewsletter@nbcuni.com And if you’re a fan, please share with everyone and anyone. They can sign up here.

Culture wars: Talarico has walked back some of the “cringey comments” he made in the past, including saying God is “nonbinary.” Expect Republicans to elevate these sort of remarks, as well as what Bernadette Breslin, the national press secretary for the National Republican Senatorial Committee, referred to as “climate alarmism.” “The problem for the Democrats excited about James Talarico is the things they like about him … make him unelectable in a Texas general election,” Breslin added. Structural advantage: It’s still Texas, which has served as a Republican stronghold for decades. “We’re feeling really confident. … Texas is one of those states that Democrats try to make really competitive,” said RNC national press secretary Natalie Baldassarre. But then reality of the state’s Republican leaning hits, she added. As for polls showing Talarico close? “As soon as the negative ads start flying, I think they’ll dip from there,” she said. Trump’s endorsement faces major tests in tonight’s primary runoffs By Ben Kamisar and Bridget Bowman Primary season may be starting to slow down, but there are still a couple of notable runoffs in South Carolina and Oklahoma tonight that will test President Donald Trump’s influence over the GOP amid a shaky August for his preferred candidates. Here are the races to watch. South Carolina Senate: Trump has expended significant political capital to boost appointed Sen. Darline Graham in this race. He appeared in the state last week for a rally, held a tele-rally last night, and his allied super PAC has spent $830,000 on texts and phone calls to voters. Graham is facing off against Rep. Ralph Norman in a primary runoff to replace her late brother on the November ballot. As Steve Kornacki notes in his “Data Dive” newsletter, Graham led 33% to 25% in the first round of voting earlier this month and finished ahead of Norman in 36 of the state’s 46 counties. But she has faced renewed scrutiny over her lack of experience in the final stretch of the campaign. Oklahoma governor: Trump also waded in here, with former state Sen. Mike Mazzei leaning heavily into the president’s endorsement as he seeks to succeed term-limited Republican Gov. Kevin Stitt. Mazzei narrowly finished second to state Attorney General Gentner Drummond in the initial June primary. Drummond has been embracing the president too: His website prominently features a photograph of him standing alongside Trump. But Trump has taken to social media in recent days to pan Drummond as a “fake Republican.” Oklahoma Senate: Even ruby red Oklahoma is hosting an ideological and generational Democratic clash. The leading vote-getter in the initial Democratic Senate primary was 31-year-old N’Kiyla Jasmine Thomas, who identifies as a democratic socialist. She’s facing 70-year-old Jim Priest, a moderate attorney and minister. Either would be a heavy underdog against Republican Rep. Kevin Hern in November. Georgia’s 13th District: There’s also a special election to serve the remainder of Rep. David Scott’s term. The race is between two Democrats: Marcye Scott, the late congressman’s daughter, and former Gwinnett County School Board Chairman Everton Blair. Scott led Blair in the preliminary primary 46% to 37%. Read more → 🎥 Tune in to the Kornacki Cam at 7 p.m. ET to watch Steve break down tonight’s results. That’s all From the Politics Desk for now. Today’s newsletter was compiled by Adam Wollner. If you have feedback — likes or dislikes — email us at politicsnewsletter@nbcuni.com And if you’re a fan, please share with everyone and anyone. They can sign up here.

articles.title: Tuesday’s Mini-Report, 8.25.26
articles.summary: Today’s edition of quick hits.
articles.body:
* Ottawa responds to the White House: "Canada struck back at the United States on Tuesday with retaliatory tariffs on about $20 billion worth of American goods, including steel, dairy products, appliances and farm equipment, as the trade war between the once-friendly neighbors escalated sharply."

* In the Middle East : "Palestinian residents of war-battered Gaza fled homes and businesses as Israeli strikes and tank fire killed at least four people Monday, including two children, hospital officials said, a week after a U.S. delegation asked Israel to draw down attacks. After evacuation warnings by Israel's military, a strike hit a building in the Bureij refugee camp in central Gaza."

* Arguably the nation's most important ongoing legal dispute : "A federal judge in Massachusetts found that the Trump administration violated her order that barred the government from moving forward with certain restrictions on mail-in voting. Yet even though she did not impose a remedy for that violation, U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani said it may ultimately benefit the voting rights plaintiffs who brought the case, because the violative government action makes it ripe to sue over."

* An unexpected trip : "Central Intelligence Agency Director John Ratcliffe made a surprise visit to Moscow on Tuesday, U.S. officials said, his first publicly known trip to the Russian capital. It came as the U.S. struggles to end Russia's invasion of Ukraine and the Iran war, although the reason for the visit wasn't immediately clear."

* The overall death toll from these boat strikes is at least 223 people: "The U.S. military killed two men in a strike against a boat in the eastern Pacific that it said was transporting narcotics, U.S. Southern Command announced early Monday. It was the first such strike by the military since June 21."

* Ukraine would benefit from help like this : "British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Monday that the U.K. will help Ukraine make its own long-range missiles by sharing classified technical information for British components."

* Aren't we due for a national conversation about this ? "Just how many N.F.L. players will end up with [the degenerative brain disease known as C.T.E.]? New data provides a sobering indication: At least one in four of all the people who have played in the N.F.L. might expect to end up with chronic traumatic encephalopathy, according to a study of hundreds of cases over a recent six-year period."

* Pirro sure does seem to lose a lot : "Jeanine Pirro, President Trump's handpicked U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, messed up the prosecution of two accused MS-13 gang leaders earlier this year. CNN reports that in April, Pirro, a former Fox News host, failed to get a jury to convict Moises Rivera-Luna, who is accused of ordering murders on U.S. soil from a Salvadoran jail cell more than 10 years ago, or his co-defendant Tokiro Rodas Ramirez, who was reportedly a local MS-13 leader in D.C."

* The administration's fixation on wall art over the last 20 months is a story unto itself: "The State Department wants to sell a painting by the celebrated artist Kehinde Wiley that the director of its Art in Embassies program called 'very woke' and 'aesthetically terrifying.' It was removed from the U.S. Embassy in the Dominican Republic last week. … State Department officials removed the painting from the embassy last week, after first hiding it behind a tarp designed with an image of the American flag."

The post Tuesday's Mini-Report, 8.25.26 appeared first on MS NOW .

articles.title: Internal watchdog finds FEMA crew violated Hatch Act by skipping homes with Trump signs
articles.summary: A Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) crew broke the law when it skipped houses with President Trump signs during Hurricane Milton recovery efforts in...
articles.body:
A Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) crew broke the law when it skipped houses with President Trump signs during Hurricane Milton recovery efforts in 2024, according to an internal government watchdog.

A new report from the Department of Homeland Security's inspector general's office determined that the crew violated the Hatch Act and FEMA policy when it skipped 11 Florida homes that indicated support for Trump, who was a candidate at the time.

It said that the incident "eroded public trust in FEMA's ability to treat everyone impartially, offer unbiased and consistent assistance, and ensure equal access to resources and tools."

The report blamed "weaknesses in FEMA's training, documentation, and oversight," saying that the agency did give crews ethics and Hatch Act training before responding to disasters.

The incident became a political flash point at the time and stoked significant GOP scrutiny of the disaster response agency. Trump eventually called for abolishing FEMA, though he later pivoted for trying to downsize it and limit aid given to states.

The Office of the Special Counsel similarly found last year that the incident in question violated the Hatch Act. A spokesperson for the inspector general's office confirmed that the new report pertains to the same incident.

The Hatch Act limits federal employees' political activities while acting in their official capacity, including barring them from using their official authority to influence election results.

Christopher Logan, FEMA's associate administrator, said that the agency no longer conducts "FEMA-led door-to-door outreach efforts."

"Staff now provide support to survivors from fixed locations determined by state and local officials through a data-informed approach," Logan wrote in an official response to the report.

He also said that after the incident, the agency gave Disaster Survivor Assistance crews mandatory Hatch Act and ethics training.

Michael Coen, who was FEMA's chief of staff during the Biden administration, said in a text message to The Hill that the report "reinforces" that the "violations were not systematic and were isolated."

"FEMA took appropriate action when the violations were briefed to senior leadership," Coen said.

The inspector general's report also notes that the office could not determine if crews skipped locations for reasons that were not allowed during other disasters because then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem did not act on FEMA's request to fund the agency's field assessment and collection tools.

The report comes after the Trump administration itself has also faced accusations of politicizing disaster aid. Politico reported earlier this year that the president had approved 23 percent of disaster funding requests from blue states and 89 percent of requests from red states.

articles.title: Dem Rep Cites Natalie Harp In Brutal Takedown Of Trump's Plan To Rename Lake Ontario
articles.summary: Rep. Debbie Dingell (Mich.) couldn’t help but name-check the aide in her scorched-earth post.
articles.body:
Michigan congresswoman Debbie Dingell had a brutal takedown of Donald Trump's idea to change the name of Lake Ontario to "Lake America" ― and, yes, it included a reference to the president's devoted aide.

Trump made the suggestion Tuesday after Canada announced it was retaliating against increased tariffs from the U.S. with some tariffs of its own.

The proposed name change was deservedly ridiculed on social media, but Dingell had a snarky suggestion of her own.

"Let's just call it Lake Natalie, so we know you'll start protecting our Great Lakes," she posted on X .

Dingell was, of course, referring to Natalie Harp, a White House aide who has penned adoring letters to Trump and repeatedly declined to get a security clearance . Harp reportedly joined the president on a small plane leaving Turkey after journalists and Cabinet members were left to fly aboard Air Force One amid a security threat last month.

Like this article? Keep independent journalism alive. Support HuffPost .

Harp has become a political lightning rod ever since Georgia Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff mentioned her in a speech last week .

"[Trump] doesn't want to do the job," Ossoff said. "He wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the emir of Qatar."

articles.title: Judge blocks Ohio from requiring proof of citizenship for voter registration
articles.summary: The court order is a blow to Republicans who have pushed to tighten voter identification requirements.
articles.body:
A federal judge on Tuesday blocked Ohio from requiring proof of citizenship when registering to vote at motor vehicles offices, a blow to Republicans who have pushed to tighten voter identification requirements ahead of the midterms.

In a 54-page opinion , U.S. District Judge Solomon Oliver Jr. said that Ohio's process for registering voters at the Bureau of Motor Vehicles requires residents to produce more documentation than what is required by the National Voter Registration Act, a federal law passed in 1993 that requires states under most circumstances to allow people to register to vote when applying or renewing a driver's license.

A requirement beyond a signed attestation to U.S. citizenship under penalty of perjury exceeds "the minimum amount of information necessary" required by the law to complete a voter registration, Oliver — a Clinton appointee — wrote.

Oliver's ruling also said the state's law offering voter registration to people when they are successfully approved for a license — as opposed to when they apply — also runs afoul of the NVRA, which is sometimes known as the "motor voter" law.

"To interpret this section of the NVRA otherwise would allow States to make registering to vote at the BMV more onerous, and could result in fewer voter registrations because the opportunity to apply was not proactively offered to otherwise eligible citizens," Oliver said in his opinion.

In 2025, Ohio GOP Gov. Mike DeWine signed an amended state motor voter statute that required residents to present documentary proof of U.S. citizenship to register to vote when applying for a driver's license at a motor vehicles office.

Two liberal advocacy organizations — Red Wine & Blue and Ohio Alliance for Retired Americans — filed a motion to block the statute's proof of citizenship requirement. The plaintiffs argued it "imposes an unnecessary obstacle to register to vote at Ohio's Bureau of Motor Vehicles offices in violation of the National Voter Registration Act."

The court order deals a timely win to Democrats who are vying to flip control of the battleground state where a coveted Senate seat, battleground House seats and a governorship that has been dominated by Republicans for the past 15 years are all up for grabs.

President Donald Trump and his allies have led a campaign to stiffen voter identification requirements and restrict mail-in voting nationwide ahead of the November midterms.

Trump's signature voting legislation, which he has called the SAVE America Act , would require a citizenship check. But it has stalled in the Senate, without enough support to pass before summer recess.

Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose, a Republican, said Tuesday that he "strongly disagrees" with the court order and will file an immediate appeal.

"I will vigorously defend our legal authority to safeguard our voter rolls and protect the integrity of Ohio's elections," he said, adding that "Ohio has a constitutional requirement to ensure that only U.S. citizens are voting in our elections."

articles.title: Trump Insider Predicts Brutal Loss for His Chosen Candidate
articles.summary: Donald Trump’s former White House press secretary has predicted that the president’s choice for Senate in South Carolina will lose Tuesday night’s Republican...
articles.body:
Donald Trump's former White House press secretary has predicted that the president's choice for Senate in South Carolina will lose Tuesday night's Republican primary.

Sean Spicer, who served in the Trump administration for the first six months of the president's first term, said on The Huddle that Rep. Ralph Norman "is going to come out ahead" of Sen. Darline Graham. Trump, 80, endorsed Graham, who is running for a full term after being appointed to replace her brother following his death in July. Even with the president's involvement, polls show the race is close.

Spicer, citing a Trafalgar poll showing Graham, 62, and Norman, 73, essentially tied at just under 48 percent, commented that it was not a good sign that Graham hadn't surpassed 50 percent, considering all that has been done for her campaign.

"They've thrown everything at it. There's a story in Politico this morning that they've spent almost a million dollars on texts, on 'get out the vote,'" Spicer, 54, said. South Carolina Sen. Tim Scott appeared on Fox News' Hannity on Monday night to try to lock up support, Spicer mentioned, and Trump flew to South Carolina last week and held a rally with Graham.

"They've thrown the kitchen sink, the trash compactor, the faucets—they've thrown everything at this race," Spicer said. "I will say, I think Ralph Norman's going to come out ahead tonight."

If that's the case, it may be due in part to some hiccups in Graham's campaign.

When asked during a debate against Norman last Tuesday whether Taiwan and the South China Sea were national security issues for the U.S., Graham said, "I'm just going to be honest here... I'm not that informed on national security."

She added: "I'm not a polished politician up here. National security is not my thing, not my area of expertise, but I support the military."

Then over the weekend, Graham took issue with a constituent recording their conversation at a campaign event, even though South Carolina is a one-party consent state.

"Is your phone recording this?" Darline asked the woman, who responded, "Yes, because, I mean, this is a political event. There's always phones recording. So, you're a politician. You know the drill."

Darline answered, "It kind of does bother me that you're recording me—I'm being honest—without my permission." A staffer then ended the conversation between the two women.

And on the eve of Tuesday's primary, Graham refused to acknowledge that Trump lost the 2020 election.

"Senator, you just mentioned that you agree with your brother on everything except for one matter, that being illegal immigration; you'd go farther than him on that," MS NOW congressional reporter Mychael Schnell told Graham. "That being said, I'm curious, do you agree with him about the 2020 election, that Joe Biden was certified the winner of that election, was lawfully elected, and that you would've voted to certify the election as your brother did?"

Graham skirted the question, saying, "I think our election system is broken." She ignored a follow-up question.

articles.title: Clinton-appointed judge triggers appeal after blocking key voter citizenship law
articles.summary: Frank LaRose vows to appeal after a Clinton-appointed judge blocked Ohio's voter registration citizenship proof law, citing federal conflicts.
articles.body: A Clinton-appointed judge in Ohio is blocking the implementation of an Ohio law that requires voting registrants to provide photo ID proof of their citizenship before enrollment. In a decision delivered on Tuesday, Judge Solomon Oliver Jr. stayed the law, citing what he saw as a conflict with federal requirements. "The court grants plaintiff’s motion for preliminary injunction … from relying on House Bill 54’s amendment to require any driver’s license or renewal to produce documentary proof of citizenship before offering the opportunity to register to vote," Oliver wrote. The decision is just the latest development in the national debate over state-level voting requirements designed to prevent non-citizens from participating in U.S. elections — and how far those requirements can go without overarching federal reforms.  FEDERAL APPEALS COURT RESTORES TEXAS MAIL BALLOT ID REQUIREMENTS IN MAJOR ELECTION INTEGRITY RULING Most immediately, the decision means that voter registrants in Ohio can once again enroll without a passport, a current driver’s license, a certification of naturalization, or a birth certificate. Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose announced on Tuesday that his office plans to appeal the decision. "We strongly disagree with that decision, and I’ve asked our legal team to file an immediate appeal. I will vigorously defend our legal authority to safeguard our voter rolls and protect the integrity of Ohio’s elections," LaRose said in a statement. In the case of Red Wine & Blue v. the Ohio Secretary of State, the court was asked to weigh whether requirements under the new Ohio law conflict with the National Voter Registration Act (NVRA), also known as the "Motor Voter Act." That law, passed in 1993 under the Clinton administration, instructs states to give voters the opportunity to register to vote using the same information they use when applying for a driver’s license. The bill was originally intended to increase voter participation. NEW JERSEY REMOVES 6,600 PEOPLE FROM VOTER ROLLS WHO WERE ELIGIBLE TO CAST A BALLOT FOR 2024 ELECTION It states that "the voter registration application portion … for a driver’s license may not require any information that duplicates information required in the driver’s license portion of the form." Notably, the NVRA doesn’t explicitly prohibit states from requiring proof of citizenship. But because virtually all driver's license forms ask about citizenship status, Oliver believes further proof amounts to redundancy. He laid out his view in Tuesday’s decision. articles.title: Meta and Google Challenge California Law Restricting Algorithmic Feed Suggestions For Minors
articles.summary: Meta and Google say that a California law restricting recommendations to minors infringes on the First Amendment.
articles.body:
The battle over California's SB 976 could set the tone nationally

Meta Platforms and Google have petitioned the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals to halt enforcement of California's Protecting Our Kids From Social Media Addiction Act (SB 976). The statute restricts social media companies from delivering algorithmically personalized recommendation feeds to minors under 18 without verifiable parental consent.

If parents do provide consent, the law places a strict default limit capping personalized feeds at one hour per day. Tech executives warn that complying with these requirements will force a complete redesign of how their digital platforms operate for young users. According to legal coverage from MediaPost, Meta warned in its filing that "absent prompt relief from this Court, Meta will have to fundamentally transform its services."

The petition follows a lower court decision by U.S. District Judge Edward Davila, who refused to block the law's personalized-feed restrictions. The tech platforms immediately appealed, arguing that algorithmic curation is a constitutionally protected editorial right.

Freedom of Expression Versus Youth Safety Concerns

The legal dispute centers on whether automated recommendation algorithms constitute expressive editorial speech protected by the First Amendment. According to reporting from Sigma Law Group, Google warned that treating automated feeds as non-expressive code carries "potentially enormous ramifications for all manner of online platforms and their users." Meta and Google maintain that curation involves editorial judgment that helps users discover relevant, high-quality content tailored to individual interests.

Conversely, state regulators and youth advocates argue that automated feeds are functional delivery mechanisms rather than protected speech. Proponents contend that infinite scroll algorithms are intentionally engineered to maximize engagement and screen time, leading to addictive habits in developing minds. They emphasize that requiring parental consent for recommendation engines is a necessary public health intervention to protect children online.

This fundamental disagreement highlights a broader tension between platform autonomy and digital child safety. If courts treat recommendations purely as technical sorting, state governments gain significantly broader authority to regulate choices. However, if algorithms are deemed protected expression, state-level restrictions face severe constitutional hurdles.

What Parents Need to Know About the National Implications

Parents across the country should recognize that the outcome of this California appeal could shape digital safety laws nationwide. If the 9th Circuit upholds the statute, similar legislative efforts limiting algorithmic feeds for minors will likely accelerate in other states.

For families, the law introduces new verification steps before teenagers can access personalized content feeds, search recommendations, or discover new creators. Additionally, the statute's built-in time caps aim to return direct control over digital media consumption back to guardians. Analysis from the American Enterprise Institute notes that the debate reflects an ongoing national showdown over balancing digital rights, minor safety, and parental authority in the modern internet era.

Ultimately, this ongoing litigation will clarify whether parents or technology platforms hold primary authority over how teenagers navigate online content. Families can expect continued changes to social media features as courts establish clear boundaries for online youth protections. Keeping informed about these legal challenges helps parents navigate evolving digital safety controls in their own households.
